div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Somehow, at this very festive season of the year, one seems not to have enough time to do all thwe things that "ought to be done," and therefore I trust all my readers have followed the advice given earlier in the season as to their over- hauling the contents of their wardrobes, and are now reaping the benefit in neat and seasonable toilettes a all sorts.

However, there is comfort to the dilatory damsels who have neglected their opportunities in viewing the many exceedingly pretty and well-made costumes which can be obtained at so many establishments, all ready save for perhaps a few alterations in tue fit of coat or • length of the skirt. _ . _

Evening gowns are generally sold with the skirt complete ready for fitting into a waist- band, while sufficient material and trimming accompanies it to be made into any style of pretty decollete bodice. The saving of time and worry is very great, and it is much more simple to select a dress to suit one's individuality as a
'very fair idea of what the dress will ultimately be when completed can be obtained by placing the skirt on a stand and draping the bodice material round the upper part of the Lay figure. . . .

A bla k satin skirt with -an overdress of flounced net is an exceedingly useful item of dress, as it can be worn with a blouse to match or one of contrasting colour. It is more chic; however, to have the bodice and skirt in har- mony.

Furs, of course, play an important part in the world of dress just at this season of the aar, and my sketch depicts the latest and most fashionable samples of muff and large collarette or pelerine. The newest muff is very large and reminds one of those favoured in the early part of the eighteenth century. In shape it should be narrower at the top growing wider towards the lower part, giving very much the appearance of a bag or satchel of immense proportions.

The very la-ge muff does not lend itself, however, very comfortably to the exigencies of ordinary mortals who have to do their shopping and pay calls on foot, with now and then the aid of a car or bus, and is really more suited to those who can afford the luxury of a carriage,
.... PICTURESQUE HAT, as it is, to say the least of it, rather cumber- some.

When one has to undertake the responsibilities of a skirt which must somehow be kept clear of mud and mire while sundry parcels demand a meed of attention, anything further which has to be carried cannot be endured at any cost, and therefore there are many women who are content to remain faithful to the smaller muff of last season.

Fur is also much used in the world of millinery, and some of the smartest toques are made entirely of one of the many varieties of fashionable fur with an osprey caught by a jewelled buckle placed erect. Hats also have furry brims, and the picturesque sample depicted is bordered with sable. A twist of brown net surrounds the crown and forms a small chon in front, from the centre of which the osprey rises. A blush-pink rose nestles under the brim at one side, and a cache-peig,ne of lace falls over the hair at the back.

There are some very smart toques made of grey squirrel trimmed with a twist of lace and some emerald green velvet. The grey fur requires some strong touch of colour to make it becoming, nnles, the wearer is possessed of an unusually brilliant complexion, when the dull tones of grey will have a softening effect
PRETTY BLOUSE.

Mink and sable are amongst the most fashionable furs employed in millinery, while the lovely soft colour of chinchilla is to be seen on some of the best models, but does not prove a good fur for hard wear as it soon loses its beautiful tone of grey and becomes yellowish if exposed to fogs and bad weather,

Moleskin is to be seen and looks especially well when used for the Russian coats caught in at the waist by an ornamental band. A pretty belt or an ornamental buckle would be found a very welcome Christmas present by most girls this season. Another useful and seasonable gift, for which there are ample opportunities for usinr„ is a pretty silk blouse made in the style illustrated. It is cut a little low at the neck and is trimmed with lace and lace in- sertion.

There are two points in the selection of a blouse for a Iriend which 'too many purchasers neglect, namely, to con-ider .not one's own taste but those of the recipient, and whether the future wearer is of a stout or slim figure. Joy has often been changed to grief when a pretty blouse has been found too tight and small in every way, and has perforce to be handed over to some slimmer relative. In spite of the frequent prophesies of its demise the blouse is still an important and very fashionable article of dress, whether it is worn in the form of the simple morning shirt, finished at the throat by- a dainty collar and cravat, or in the smart afternoon blouse of silk and lace. a For theatre or evening wear it is expressed in lace, net, chiffon and silk, used singly or inter- mingled one with another. A plain black cloth skirt is a very useful possession as it can be worn with any kind of blouse whether simple or elaborate, and always looks well.
COQUETTE.

div.head: Examiner, Friday, December 19, 1902.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, December 19, 1902.
A WARRINGTON SENSATION. ( Copyright.) IRMA'S WOOING. WOMAN CHARGED WITH CAUSING HER HUSBAND'S DEATH. Medical Evidence Results in her Discharge.

Some sensation was created in Warrington on Sunday when it became known that a woman named Susannah ' Flavell, residing at 19, Stamford-street, had been arrested on the .charge of causing the death of her husband, Thomas Flavell, a puddler. It appears that a drunken quarrel occurred at the house on Friday night, and it was alleged that Mrs. Flavell threw an empty jug at the deceased, inflicting an ugly wound on the side of the head. The man was taken to Dr. Curtis's surgery. where the woundwaedressed by Dr. Batchan,and Flavell was told to call again on the following morning. He failed to do so, and during the day went to the works where he was employed and obtained his wages. After- wards he visited a public-house, and when his adopted child, Walter Hall, came home at ten o'clock at night he found him lying asleep on the floor. The boy placed a pillow under his head, and after a time, noticing that he had stopped snoring, again went to him and found that he was dead. Dr. Curtis was sent for and made an examination, and early on Sunday morning the woman was taken into custody. However, a post-mortem examination revealed the fact that death was simply due to heart failure, and was not accelerated by the wound. Consequently the prisoner was discharged on Tuesday morning.
PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. THE STORY OF THE QUARREL.

The prisoner, Susannah Flavell, appeared before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates, on Monday, charged with unlawfully causing the death of her husbaad by striking him on the head with a jug, at 19, Stamford- ' street, on Friday night. Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner was charged on suspicion with causing the death of her husband, a puddler, who lived with her at 19, Stamford- street. Between seven and eight o'clock on Friday night, the deceased came home, after having finished his day's work, and found the prisoner on the sofa, under the influence of drink. They had a quarrel because there was no tea ready, and they remained quarrelling for some time, and then the deceased, it was alleged, struck the prisoner with his hand across her mouth. The prisoner picked up an empty jug, whichwas lying on the table, and threw it at the deceased. It caught him on the side of the head, and he lost a great deal of blood. He was taken to Dr. Curtis's surgery in Bewsey-road. where the wound was dressed, and he went home and was put to bed. He was told to call at the doctor's next tnoming,but failed to do so, and at noon went to the works for his wages. Subsequently he visited a public- house,and commenced drinking, and at about 10.30 on Saturday night he was found lying on the heartbrug in his own house. The prisoner was then on the sofa,under the influence of drink. Flavell was snoring,and his adopted child, who happened to come in, put a pillow under his head. Shortly afterwards he ceased to snore, and the boy, becoming suspicious, called in a neighbour, and it was found that Flavell was dead. Sergeant Evans also visited the house. He (Superintendent Monaghan) askedl for a remand until 'Tussday morning, as the inquest was to be held that (Monday) afternoon. The application was granted. THE INQUEST. DEATH DUE TO HEART FAILURE. -

Mr. F. A. Jones, Deputy Coroner, conducted the inquest on the body of Thomas Flavell at the Police Station on Monday afternoon. At the outset, Mr. Jones related the police report on the case, and added that the Coroner ordered a post- mortem examination, the result of which would be laid before the jury. When they had heard the medical evidence he thought that the inquiry into the alleged assault would be considerably shortened. The first witness was Walter Hall, aged sixteen years deceased's adopted son. He stated that deceased .was 38 years of age and was a native of Bilston, Stafford- shire. Witness came home shortly after seven o'clock on Friday evening and found his mother asleep. His father, who was sitting by the lire, complained of having had no tea. His mother shortly afterwards awoke. Both his father and mother were under the influence of drink and they had some words. Witness went out to a band practice and when he returned about nine o'clock deceased and his mother had some more words about there being no tea ready. Witness asked them to have no bother and said he would bring somechips. He went out for the chips but soon after his sister followedhim and in consequence of what she told him he went home. He found his father sitting on a chair by the fire. His head was bent down and blood was flowing from the right temple. His mother was on the stairs crying. Lying on the floor near his father's chair were the pieces of , jug produced. His mother came into the kitchen and ' said: "I am sorry, but he should not have started o me while I was on the sofa." His father said "I wiln have her locked up for this." Witness asked his fatb/r. 'Who has done this?" and he replied "Why, her." The wound, which bled a great deal was dressed by D , Batchan at Dr. Curtis!s surgery, and deceased was told to call at the surgery again next morning. He failedto do so, remaining in bed until noon. Witness went with him to draw his wages and afterwards left him at the "Three Pigeons" public house. He did not see deceased again until shortly after ten on Saturday night, when witness returned home. His mother was then asleep on the sofa and deceased was lying on the floor. Think- ing that he was sleeping off the effects of drink witness put a pillow under his head. Deceased seemed to be snoring. After a time witness noticed that he stopped breathing and going to him found he was dead. He then roused his mother. His father and mother drank a great deal, and quarrelled sometimes; and last week deceased gave his wife a black eye. Dr. Curtis said he was sent for on Saturday night to go to Stamford-street about 20 minutes to twelve, and when he got to the house of the Flavells he examined, the man and found that life was extinct. Acting on the instructions of the coroner, he made a post-mortem examination of the body of the deceased on Sunday night, assisted by Dr. Batchan and Dr. Smith. Deceased's heart was enlarged, and the stomach was distended and full of peas. The cause of death was heart failure, con- sequent on an enlarged heart and probably aggravated by over-distention of the stomach. They considered that the wound, which was a small superficial punctured wound a sixth of an inch in depth, had nothing to do with the cease of death. Death would have taken place when it did if there bad been no wound, provided that deceased had been drinking like he did on the Saturday. He should say that the enlargement of the heart was caused by alcoholism. The Foreman: Would excitement have aggravated or hastened the death or interfered with the heart's action. Dr. Curtis :—I should say not. The Deputy-Coroner said that if the jury accepted the evidence which had been given by the doctor, it dis posed of any question as to the assault committed byr the wife. It seemed to be useless to call witnesses, afte the evidence of the doctor. . _
-- --- The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence.
PRISONER DISCHARGED.

The woman was again brought before the Court on Tuesday. Superintendent Monaghan informed the Bench that the post-mortem examination showed that the wound had nothing to do with the cause of death, and the prisoner was discharged.
By ELLEN TIGHE HOPKINS, Author of "A Lost Lover," "Jack and Jill, "When • I was Twenty," "Will He Win Her ? " "Reality," Ac.

div.head: "A NEW LEASE OF LIFE." Sensational Bile Bean Cure. Depression, Constipation and Debility Ended. A Woman's Message to Women.
div.p: "A NEW LEASE OF LIFE." Sensational Bile Bean Cure. Depression, Constipation and Debility Ended. A Woman's Message to Women.

Women in middle life have in the case of Mrs. Hannah Gill. of Park Gate Farm, Emlev, near Wakefield, sensa- tional proof of the value of Chas. Forde's Bile Beans. Interviewed by a Wakefield Herald reporter, she said:— "I have been ill altogether for some si x or seven years. At times I was so bad that I could neither eat nor drink, work nor sleep. My flesh and my bones seemed to ache all over, my memory left me and I used to wander about like one lost. I was also greatly troubled with costiveness, and my food seemed to do me no good. I used to fancy I could eat all sorts of things, but when I got them I could never enjoy them. I was also subject to terrible sweats, although all the time I was shivering and starving. "My neighbours told me it WAS due to the change of life, and to me it was a change and no mistake. Why, instead of enjoying life as I had been accustomed to do, I wished many a morning after a long and restless night that I might rest in death before the day closed. Sleep? Why no ,• on going to bed I might doze for an hour or so, but after that there was no repose for me. You will know how bad I really was when I tell you that on being removed to the house of a married daughter for change, I imagined myself in an asylum, and would not allow them to fasten the room door. Even when I was at home with my husband and family I could not believe somehow that it was my home. 'Of course I was seen by the doctor who gave me medicine and told me to keep quiet, but his medicine did me very little good. "One day my sister advised me to try Chas. Forde's Bile Beans. I began to take them and you can imagine my joy to find about three weeks after commencing with them, that my memory had returned. I began mending straight off. I also began to sleep. Altogether I pulled up veryquickly. I continuedtaking a couple of Bile Beans every night for some time longer until I was quite well again. "I have had 12 children, and 20 grandchildren, and'a healthier family never breathed. lam now 55 years of age. but I feel as bright and buoyant as when twenty." Chas. Forde's Bile Beans may belied from all chemists or post free from the Bile Bean Manufacturing Co., Red Cross-street, London, E.C., upon receipt of prices or 2s. 9d. For depression, nausea, indigestion, liver and kidney ailments and the disorders common to women in middle life, they are without equal.

div.head: CHAPTER lIL
div.p: CHAPTER lIL

It was nearly a fortnight after that before I was able to go down the village again to see the home folks. Lady Isabella had been worse than usual, and though she often begged me to go out a little, and not to think so much of her, I did not care to leave her. I understood her needs, and her wishes,
more quickly than anyone else, and very gladly remained by her to give what little ease and help I

; could. But one evening, after tea, she fell into a I quiet Bleep; and, telling Harris to watch that no one disturbed her, I put on my things and ran down home, to see how they were getting on under the new and strange state of affairs. Father had been no laggard in the arrangement of his new property. I had received a deed two days before whie conveyed to me the sum of twenty. thovisa.nu pounds absolutely. Father had divided. hi fortune equally amongst us, keeping one-fifth as his own share, and giving a fifth to etch of us. Sam's and Miriam's shares were to be held in trust until they were of age. Paul and I were to do as we pleased with oars. Father had no more belief than I had in the power of money to give happiness. He knew well the dangers of wealth, but he did not fear that either Paul or I would come to harm through possessing money. We might give it away foolishly, but that would not have troubled him greatly. Father had found his own happiness in we rk, not in idle luxury. I was rather doubtful how it would suit him and mother to be rich. It had been a bright, clear autumn day, but the sun was low on the horizon, and the white mists were rising over the distant meadows when I reached the cottage. Mother was standing at the garden gate looking down the road, with one hand, shading her eyes from the low rays of the sun. She was a little woman, hardly reaching to father's shoulder, with smooth, brown hair, and brisk, methodical ways. But she did not seem brisk to- day; I had rarely seen her look so troubled, even when the bread would not rise properly. But she, brightened up when she saw me, and kissed me warmly. After awhile I asked what troubled her. She laughed as she answered: "I suppose it's the money, child. Don't, for goodness' sake, tell Miriam ; but the heart's gone out of life, Rachel. I used to be so proud of my cutting and contriving; so pleased when I got thirteenpennyworth out of a shilling; and now my occupation's gone. There seems no heart in doing anything. Your father says I may spend what I like, and I needn't work; but, dear me, I can't begin at my time of life to sit idle and learn to spend without counting the cost!" "I shouldn't try, mother. Father likes whatever you like; and if you prefer to be busy about the place, he won't say anything against it. "No, he wouldn't; but Sam and Miriam would. They want father to buy this house, for he won't hear of living in any other, and build on to it, and be gentlefolks; and the friends I'velknown all my life will be afraid to set foot imile my grand house, and the gentlefolks will never came, and we shail fall between two stools." And mother was really very near tears, but she lam g..ed it off. "It seems too ridiculous to be sorry at having a comfortable fortune," she said, "but I really am, Rachel ; I was happier as we were. It don't seem to matter now whether I gat up in the morn- ing or lie in bed, and tlibt's a begaeleas sort of feeling ; but perhaps I shall get used t it." "You will get other interests presently, mother; now, I am sure you would like veiy much to take Barton's old farmhouse that is teimding empty, and furnish it plainly, and make it a sort of holiday home for poor children from London tc come and get some country air. Yu u might have five or six at a time all the year round. .Betty
Marrow, who lias just lost her husband, .would bo . .

thankful to take her little girl and live in the house and look after the club-lien, and you could go every day, and I daresay m ',I-1y of the children would want clothes that :%ou could make them." "That would be just what I should delight in, Rachel. I'll talk to father about t to-night. How the children would lo.e these ii.dols and parks!" "And in winter they could I are swings in that big barn, if it were mended motile, and a dance at Christmas to father's violin, and all the pleasure and comfort would be your dot Mother's face was radiant w tit this idea, and I knew my children's holiday I ore would soon be safely started and growing ;'sbe happy in helping , to get it into working o der. And by the time Miriam left school she would have become more accustomed . to money, and the troubles its possession entails. We were turning into the house to make some tea, but stopped a moment as we heard a.quick, firm step coming down the lane, to• see who it could be. There were not many passengers along that lane beyond the slouching village folk. The step came quickly up to the gate and stopped. It was Paul. I, had not seen him since the evening I first heard about the money, when he told me of his adoration for Miss Irma. He was in a plain snit of dark tweed, with a deerstalker sort of hat. I should hardly have known him had I met him in a crowd, he looked so handsome and gentleman- like. Mother and I, both speaking at once, asked • him where he was going. "I am come to say good-bye," he said. "I have just posted you a letter, Rachel, I hardly hoped to see you here. I have to catch the 5.30 trnin, my higagge is gone on to the station." "Have you left the Rectory, Paul? " "Yes, mother. If you don't hear from me for some months, don't be anxious. I shall be all right. God bless you." He kissed us both and was gone, his face alight with hope. I watched his strong, upright figure walking rapidly away down the lane. I was very fond of my brother Paul. Did / wish that the money had never come to us? I almost think I did. Mother and I turned and looked at each other, as Paul's footsteps died away in the distance. ' "Where can he be going, Rachel?" she asked, looking bewildered, and a trifle troubled. "That money is like antearthquake ; it will break up our happy home life I know it will. I wish, with all my heart, it had never come to us! Miriam was giddy enough before, and Sam is talking about keeping a -hunter, tind Paul off no one knows where. " :"Paul will Come to no harm. mother; don't fear for him; and father will guide Sam. and Miriam wisely ; they are a little off their heads just now with the suddenness of it all, but they will soon find out that money brings its troubles as well as its pleasures. As you get older, mother, you will he glad to be able to have a servant and tt nice biome without father's working; and he will love some day to go up to London and hear the great I don't see why you shouldn't propose to him to go up for a week now, and take Sam and Miriam with yoa and just see a few things." "Why, Rachel I've no finery fit for London."

"And 'you don't want finery, Mother.. A feW quiet handsome things for you and Miriam will make you presentable anywhere. Don't let Mitiam run to cheap finery, mother, and it will be all right,. And you and f ither go wherever you cal with .Sam and Miriam until they have recovered their halentie. Fa will see it is all right if you will help hint in the beginning." "Couldn't you .come. Rachel ? " "I can't leave my lady just now," I answered; but I was glad to see mother was not altogether' averse to the idea of goinT. "I might come up for a few honra whilst you aro there." "Sam would Want 03 tugo to the theatre," said mce her, with a fa:l9 in which doubt and excitement mingled somewhat comically. "Of couree he would," I replii d, laughing, "ar.L. it would be much better for you all toiO together ; hold together, mother, whatever you do. Share their pleasures' as far as you possibly can till they've gat a tittle. used to the new life; and ne harm will come of the money." "But I've no iheatre gowns, Rachel." "You would only wan, come good lace, mother, over.yone black silk ; ree lace, and 13 theatre wraF or cloak. Miriam (tut get an evening blouse mid opent cape in ten minutes. Father and Sam must. helm evening clothes;, these must be made 'for them." Mother,fairiv lief:bed outright this time. "Well I never." she said, "it will be funny. I doubt but we'll enjoy it after all." I. mit suri,you will." I said, "so long as yoo keep to;ether, and don't lose your heads overspend- ing. it is rather like drinking, and apt to get the apperhand." "I should never agree to that, 'Rachel, you may be full sure. rinean to have my holiday home, and every poor child I see in London will remind me of it:"

Mother was looking 'quite bright and cheerful. and I felt sure that she would carry out all my suggestions to the full. Mother was usually the practical leaa:ng spirit in our home. Father was the somewhat dreamy musicain, generally ready to fall in with her proposals, very rarely suggesting anything out of the beaten track himself. I could see by mother's smile that her thoughts were busy with the new plans I had put into her head, and pleasantly busy with them, too, as she sat, tea-cup in hand, gazing out of the window with a very pre- occupied look. But suddenly the smile vanished, and the colour mounted in her face. She set down her cup hastily. . _ . _
"Ittithel, there's Mrs. Bathurst and Miss Irma at tly gate! Whatever shall I d 9? And the tea- in the best parlour!" &

I 'laid my hand 'on hers as she was about to riee hurriocily from her chair and laughed quietly. "Where should the tea-things be at this time of day bat in the best parlour, mother? Nothing could be more fortunate. There's a good cup of tea in the pot, and nothing at the Rectory can beat your home-made cake. Just make them welcome, mother, that is everything you need do. Keep cool and make them welcome. Tll give them tea. If your china isn't egg-shell it is old and good." As I spoke I went into the passage in answer to Miss 'mo peremptory impetuous rat- tat.. If she had been calling at Buckingham Palace she would have given the same impatient rap. .The door stood wide Open, Eli mother .and I had left it when we entered.

"0 Rachel," she exclaimed. "we have come to make love to your rich mother. Mamma is in the pony carriage. (ay I bring her in? " "To be sure," I answered. "Mother will be delighted." She went swiftly back to the carriage and helped her mother to alight, and I watched her with pleasure. Her, dress was of the simplest, a rough ruddy tweed of perfect make, skirt and coat alike,. but there was the faint rustle as she walked, which ,told of unseen silk, and lace-edged skirts flashed about her slim feet as she held her dress away from the carriage wheel. I loved to watch Irma as I loved to watch , a sunset. Everything about her was bright, vivid, dainty, and ever changing. Her great charm to me was her changefulness. She was not fickle or unstable, but her moods were always varying—always unexpected. Her mother had been a hanthome woman, but was growing 'stout, and a trifle cumbrous. Her dress, like her knanner, was much More assertive than Irma's ; the Otall-mark was not so conspicuous in the mother as in the,danghter, and attention had to be drawn to the fact that it was there. This was done—or attempted—by means of many rings and bangles, and much heavy jet which danced and glittered at every turn._ _ .
"Good afternoon, Miss Howard," she exclaimed pleasantly. ."Irma and I thought we ought to come and see how your mother is bearing her misfortunes."

"She feels then .a good deal, Mrs. Bathurst," I replied, adopting her light tone, !'and was jiast fortifying herself with tea. Do come in." Having established her 'comfortably on our rather roomy sofa, and mother beside her, I turned to look after Miss Irma, bat I found her already quite at home in my chair, busily pouring out tea. "That is for m imam," she said, handing me a cup; "she likes sugar and no milk. May I give you a cup, Mrs. Howard? Do you take sugar? I do so like pouring out toy'. We have it handed round at the Rectory; it is such a stupid way. This is such a darling pot,' it seems inexhaustible. What a very scrumptious cake, Rachel; may I have 'another piece? Is that blEckberry jam? It looks delicious. I should like some on my cake, please. I must take off my gloves. I have spent all my quarter's allowance, and we are not in November yet. I don't know how I can make my gloves last out till Christmas.' Isn't it very nice to have a great lot of nioney. Rachel ? " she added, laying her soft little hand on mine as I sat beside her; and before I could reply she Went on in a low tone: "Paul has gone away. Rachel, and we miss him so much. I am glad you all have a fortune, but it upsets people, rather, doesn't it ?'‘ And to my utter amazement she suddenly began to cry, and took a little cambric handkerchief with a yellow border from her jacket-pocket and sobbed into it passionately. Mother and Mrs. Bathurst ceased their talk and looked aghast. I knelt down beside Irma and ' put my arms round her waist and exclaimed: "Whatever is It?"

But before I could say more she held up a laughing face with the tear-drops on her long lashes, and, stuffing the little wet handkerchief into her pocket again, she said: "It was the blackberry jam, Rachel fit is so intoxicating. Do give me a little more on one of those wee crisp biscuits." "Indeed," I said, as I weakly gave her the biscuit well piled, "I, think you have had quite enough." "Let us go and wash up, Rachel," she said, popping the dainty morsel.; into her round open mouth and jumping up from her chair. ' And before I could remonstrate she had swiftly packed up the china and carried off the tray to the kitchen. "Where is Miriam ? " she asked, as she set it down on the white deal table, and looked round admiringly at the bright pots and pans. "Oh, what a nice, clear fire; is' a pity we did not make some buttered toai And what a delicious little pipkin. Shall I make you some toffee in this, Rachel? I can make lovely toffee. I gave Paul some one day, and he said it was the best he had ever tasted.'

"I think we had better clew- away one mess before we make another," I said, glancing at the tea-tray. "Very well," she said, a little regretfully. "You wash and I'll wipe. Isn't it very nice to be rich, Rachel? Are you an rich, or only your father—l mean, has he given you any money to have quite for yourself? "Yes, he has given us all some," I replied. "A good lot?" she asked w"' :fly. "Yes," I said smiling, "a good lot." "I expect you will all be going away now-P" "No," I said, "lye shall not. This will always be home. Father is going to buy this house." Her face brightened inunediately, and throwing down the tea-cloth he commenced a barn dance up and down the tiled kitchen.

"Come and do a barn dance, Rachel. Miriam can wash up when she comes home. Oh, there is mamma getting into the carriage; I shall be left behind. Good-bye, Rachel, I am so glad you are going to buy this house " ' • and she threw her arms round my neck and hugged me with an impetuosity which nearly tumbled my hair over my shoulders, and rim to the carriage and drove off so quickly that the boy nearly got left behind. "She is sweetly. pretty," said mother, "and Mrs. Bathurst is really very hind and friendly. She is izoing to get up a bazaar for the new organ fund. She says I can afford to give her a few things now." "You can alTord to gives her the whole bazaar, mother, if you like, or the organ, for that matter."
And we both laughed heartily, and went in and washed up the tea-things Miss Irma had left un finished. , '
We'laughed again as we washed and dried the cups. It was such a comical idea for mother, whore pride and ambition all her life had been to make her Sunday beef last over the third day!

div.head: CHAPTER IV.
div.p: CHAPTER IV.

I was glad afterwards that I had had that talk with mother• for it, did not chance to me to see her , again for smite time. For several weeks I scarcely rrossed the threshold of Lady Isabella,'s studio, and never once passed the park gates of the Chase. A Eurried breath of air in the early morning or late evening was all I could snatch. 'Lady Isabella was very and Harris end I both had our hands till. Day and night we took turn 'and turn about •• ease her sufferings, with a little help occasionally from the housekeeper. Lady Isabella did not like 4'A-singers about her: And I best understood her ri,.•eas in these sharp attacks of pain, which were gradually relining the potter's clay, and loosening the silver cold. She hoped it was So: -

"The veil grows thinner, Rachel," she said to me one night, her, pain wrung face aglow with hope. • • - And I was glad in the midst of my regret. The Pr was so sharp, the long hours of the crucifixion so terrible. Nevertheless, she got better orym more, and was able again to lie on the sofa in the studio window, and idle with her paint-brushes, or draw a few set long notes, that were more sad than gay, from my violin,

...... Sir George had paid her daily visits throughout her illness, tip-toeing noisily into the room before he went out of a morning, and creaking carefully in to say gnat-night.. 'She never -answered his condolence aho.,t her health, hut ..responded with sympa, betic inquiry about his spirt, or his more pel'son:l pursuits, to which he would reply with gusto and then tip-toe out again. 0 it came to Pass that we were within sight cf Cliristma efore r could give thought to my own affairs, or dream of taking that day in town which mother and I had counted on. '
They had all gone to town as we planned it. Mother had grasped the nettle with true English

They were all keeping their heads well, so far as I could judge, but I was beginning to long badly to see them. _

And just at the right moment Mr. Gerald came home on a fortnight's leave. With her son in and out of the studio all day, and Harris at hand in case of need, I might be spared for a few hours. I thought Mr. Gerald did not look well, and he certainly was not in his usual spirits. I wondered had Miss Irma anything to do with it. But I could not see that she had, for the first day be was home he went to the Rectory tb lunch and brought her back with him' to tea, and they teased and bantered each ether as they always did when together. But they both looked pale, and I even fancied their gaiety and fun ,was a little forced. After tea Miss Irma came and sat on my lap as she was sometimes fond of doing, and laid her round cheek arotinst mine. "How can you stay all your life in this room, Rachel? Why don't you go and spend your money, you miser." "I am going to-morrow." "Are your really, Rachel? " she exclaimed, springing off my lap as suddenly as she had descended upon it. "Where are you going, and for how long, and what are you going to buy ? " And she knelt down before me, and laying her arms across my lap scanned my face with eager interest. "I am going to town for a few hours to buy 2pkies," I answered demurely. "0 Rachel, how entrancingly interesting"; and her blue eyes grew absolutely dark with delight. "Cakies for my Sunday-school girls and—my family," I added, busily disentangling wool, and only glancing at her swiftly. But she took my face between her two little fists and made me look straight into her eyes. "And cakie for your friends, Rachel? Take me with you, Rachel, I am so dull at home—now." ' "Why now ?" I exclaimed in surprise. "In the middle of the hunting season, and with Christmas so near, and the hunt-ball; why it is the gayest time of the dear." "I am tired of all those foolish things," she answered, twisting my wool into a worse tangle than ever. "I want to' do something useful, and sensible."

"Like buying cakies," I suggested. But she only took me by the shoulders and pre- tended to shake me very roughly, and then ran away to the piano and began singing "Little Alabama Coon." And we all joined in the plain- tive chorus, Lady Isabella's soft contralto, and Mr. Gerald's deep bass, forming a fine back- ground for the clear gay soprano. "Go to sleep, my little piccaninny, The bogie man will catch yon if you don't Slumber on the bosom of your old Daddy Jimmy, Daddy's going to whack you if you don't."

div.head: CHAPTER V.
div.p: CHAPTER V.

I reached Baker-street about noon the next day. I found mother alone in a pretty suite of rooms in Nottingham-place, eagerly expecting me. She was the same mother as ever, and yet she would never be the same again. She had quickly adapted her- self to her new life, once fairly started on it, and I turned her round and admired her with all my heart; and then we settled to talk, I had so much to hear. Miriam was going daily to Queen's College, in Harley-street. Mother said she had settled to her studies at once, and was getting on ' well, but she was anxious about Sam. "Why?" T asked. "He has gone crazy over engineering and electricity." "He might have gone crazy over worse things," I said. "How, Rachel?" "Well, horse-racing, or ballet dancers, or cards," I replied. "Well, of course," said mother, "so he might; I never thought of that. Father took him one day to see some big engineering works at Westminster, and since then he has been for seeing everything; and to-day they are gone to some electric works in Goshawk-road, wherever that is. Sam wants to be apprenticed, or articled, or whatever they call it." "He couldn't do better." I said. "He has found his vocation, perhaps." "That's what father said. He is immensely interested; not but what he loves' the theatres and conceits too. We have begn .many times, but always all of us together." ' "That's right, mother." "It's really hard work, Rachel, shopping and pleasuring. Many nights I have crawled to bed far more tired than on a washing-day." "Poor mother, it's only for a while; then you can return to country air and rest." "But I rather like it, Rachel, all the same." And we both laughed at the confession, and mother continued: "Father and Sam look spiendid in evening clothes, Rachel. I had no notion clothes made such a difference; and really I thought last night Miriam was nearly as pretty as Miss Irma. We went to a concert at the Albert Hall, and bought her such a pretty frock of soft whiteasilk,' all smocked' like a child's, and she has a pink opera-cloak trimmed with white feather trimming. .They will all be home to tea. Can't you stay one night with us, Rachel ?" I shook my head. "I can stay until after tea, mother, but mat later. I want you to come out with me after lunch to do some shopping in. Bond-street." "Yes, I shall like to go with you. I find it very clitieult to get used to saying lunch" and te eating late dinner,, Rachel. It's a nasty unwhole- some time of day to be .eating one's diviner. I always get mine in the middle of the day if I can. I ordered .a pheasant for us to day at lunch-time, Rachel, I thought you'd like it, and we can make it our dinner ; the others Will want theirs when they come home later." "Have you heard from Paul, mother?" "Not a word, It tchel. Where can he be? It's n-,t very kind of him." "lie has some special reason, Cleiend on it, , mother. We shall know in good time." I hardly knew what purpose was in my mind when I started out with mother about three o'clock to look at the most fashionable London btreets. We had enjoyed a long intimate talk together, such as strengthens the .hearts of women, and I had insp ct al with keen interest and amusement the many purcunses made by the quarteit since they had been in town.' Knowing them all so intimately as I did, I could follow the characterist ice of each one in the purchases. Mother's leaning to useful and substantial clothing, her wide thought for the needs of the poorer friends who had been our lifedong neighbours, and for the still nooser friends she hoped soon to have under her iCrotec- tion in her hot diy home. Father's refined love of • music and the dramaiwas_shewn in a few beautiful engritvings, and two exquisite little statuettes, one pf Mendelsohn, one of Henry Irving. Miriam 's girlish love of finery, I hoped, would- he tempered presently, by t.ssociation, and by mother's and father's example. For Sam's new craze I was deeply thankful. It would provide him with a pro- fession, an amb:tion, a full use for his, time and his money, and save bim front possible &Moralisa- tion. I urged mother strongly .td, let him have his will in such a healthy direction. Sam may develop into a great inventor, wlto,knows ? I decided that I Would evince the keenest interest in all his hooks,, and in his most extravagant, models when he shewetl.them to me. We wandered the length of Baker-street, but I tvas not tempted: We turned into Oxford-street and proceeded in leisurely fashion, talking as we went, to Oxford6circus, and - down Regent-street, glancing this side and that as we edged our way amidst the brisk crowd intent upon shopping. It was a dark grey December day, not too cold; a day when in London the dusk falls rapidly, 'and already the gas was being lighted in the big shop windows, showing up the tempting wares. But none of the wares came up to the ideal that was floating somewhere in the recesses of my mind. We turned down Conduit-street and crossed into New Bend-street, and in less than a minute I knew what it Nsas I had been seeking. (To be continued.)

div.head: GUA I 11A
div.p: GUA I 11A
VENEZUELA, THE LAND OF STRIFE.

The South American Republics are all addicted te disturbance, but none more so than Venezuela. Since 1847, the country has scarcely known what peace or legality is. She began with a twenty- three years' struggle between the Liberals and the Conservatives which left the llanos ruined for years, and the credit of the country completely destroyed. Between 1870 and 1889, Gillman Blanco was Dictator, and the country was com- paratively tranquil, but of legal government there was not a shadow. Civil war broke out in 1892, and since then half the land has ban in a state of anarchy. Palacio, the successor of Blanco, was overthrown by General Crespo in that year, but the only held office for a few months. His successor, General Alverez, soon had to make way for the reinduction of Crespo, who sought popularity by picking a quarrel with Great Britain over the Guiana frontier. Nevertheless, his dictatorship was con tested by successive revolts, and in 1898 General Ignacio Andrede became President. His positior was not less contested than that of his predecessors and in August, 1899, the present Dictator, General Cipriano Castro, organised a revolution and expelled Andrede.
VEN:
r ELAN CONGRESS AND SENATE CR4IMBER, CARACAS.

Castro is a Cazique by birth, the son of a farmer, who live in the village of Capacho, in the province e Tachira. He is only thirty-six years of age. His education was not very elaborate, and his knowledge of affairs was confined to what he had manage to learn while acting as clerk to a German firm at Maracaibo. He has, however, managed to keep the upper hand over the rebellious factions in the country. His position as President, when in - hostile contact with two nations such as Great Britain and Germany, could not be said to be enviable when it is considered how bellicose is the public opinion by which he is supported in office, Lad bow averse t at public opinion would naturally be to any peaceable settlement.

This wonderful man, '*ho is now well on in middle life and turning grey, is as vigorous as ever, and well able to take the prominent part that falls to him in the performance; and he is never known to spare himself,despite increasing age and the number of years he has been at work. The main features of the show will be the • same as formerly —lndian dances and attacks, cowboys mani- pulating their lassoes and taming buck jumpers, and the attack on the mail - coach, which was al- ways the popular finale of the whole. Amongst the new ones the most interesting promises to be Indipm village, with the red men them- selves, their squaws, and their pappooses living their native life in wigwams. Many of these very Indians fought against the encroachment of civi- lisation as recently as 1891 in the reballion of the Pine Ridge Agency, which was the final effort of the Sioux, tribe; and some of them are of the stock of the famous Red Cloud, who is known as the Nana Sahib of the Western Plains, and was for years the De Wet of the prairies. Another interesting addition is a band of Mexican Ruralies, who combine the business of mounted policeman and cowboy, and divide theio time between running down horse thieves or recalcitrant Indians and lassoing wild horses

div.head: DRURY LANE PANTOMIME.
div.p: DRURY LANE PANTOMIME.

First of all the annual Christmas shows comes Drury Lane, which is always a great event at Yule- tide, and one looked forward to as eagerly by grown-up people as by the children, who are pro- fessedly catered for ; and each year the manage- ment at this famous theatre seems to try to go one better than the year before in general magnificence and great stage effects: This year promises to be aio exception to the rule ; and for some weeks there has been much talk about "Mother Goose," the subject of this year's pantomime, and never has the advance booking been so prodigious, the receipts ahead) beating all records up to date by many thousands of pounds. "Mother Goose, which has not been used ince Sir Augustus Harris's production in 1880, has been thoroughly brought up to date, and wiH be produced in three parts, an innovation which will be greatly appreciated by the eider portion of the audience. There are to be twelve scenes, of which the principal ones from a spectacular point of view will be the proces,ion of the "Art. Noveltieiof the World," the "Lind of Heartsease" (in .which everyone will be dressed as a pansy, and the colour effect promises to be splendid), and the scene in Gooseland, where everybody will be geese, and there will be a prodigious goose ballet, which

Attould prove highly amusing. The book will be /by Mr. Arthur Collins and Mr. J Hickory Wood, and the music by Mr. J. M. Glover, who wields the .stonduCtor's baton at Drury Lane. As usual, Mr. Dan Leno and Mr. Herbert Campbell will be in the principal r Es. as "Mother Goose" and "her sou Jacky" respectively. At one time it was rumoured during his serious illness in the summer that the former would be missing from the caste for the Sr.t time for many years ; but fortunately he has couirdetelY recovered his strength, and is able to go through even such a trying ordeal as a Drury Lane pantomime run. Miss Madge Lessing, who made a success two years ago in The Sleeping Beauty," will again be : 'principal girl," .while Miss Maude Beatty, an Australian importation with a big Colonial :reputation, wilt make her dibet in England as principal boy." The number of the minor parts de legion; and it is said that at least twenty 'thousand pounds is being spent on the Brobdingn- agian production, which promises to be a greater success than ever. .

div.head: BUFFALO BILL AT OLYMPIA.
div.p: BUFFALO BILL AT OLYMPIA.

Another show which promises to rival even Drury Lane in popularity is Buffalo Bill's Wild West, which opens at Olympia on Boxing Night, and many look back upon their visit to Earl's Court some years ago with remembrance of unusual interest. The majority of Colonel Cody's stock-in-trade—lndians, cowboys, Cossacks, horses and buffaloes—arrived at Addison Road ten days ago. and since then the remainder have been turning up in driblets, while Buffalo Bill himself, the centre-piece of this great show, is expected by the end of this week to put the final touches to the arrangements.

div.head: ALEXANDRA PALACE VELODROME.
div.p: THE ALEXANDRA PALACE VELODROME.

The great central hall at the Alexandra Palace in North London, has been fitted with one of the largest indoor cycle tracks in the world. A good idea of the construction of this track, which has been named the Velodrome, is afforded by our illustration, and the size will be realised when it is stated that there are only twelve laps to a mile. As viewed from the grand orchestra, from which our sketch was mvde, racing is, to say the least, exciting, especially as the men take the steep bankings. These rise almost perpendicularly for

THE VELODROME, THE ONLY INDOOR CYCLE RACING TRACK IN EUROPE. about five feet, and then slope off in a half circlet making the total height ten feet six inches. The whole track is removable' being built in sections; it has to be removed upon occasions when concerts, etc., are heid in the hall. As a novelty, the racing, which is to be a regular feature, is sure to attract, esp,cially as some of the best of our home and continental cracks will be there. The Velodrome is the only indoor track in Europe, for there has not been any boom in this particular form of rscing since the Olympia days in the 'mid-nineties. In America there are several covered, tracks or colosseums. 'notably that at Madi:son Square Gardens, New York. The manager of the Alexandra Park Velodrome, Mr. Gus Hart, and his assistant, Jack Camp, secured for the inaugural races several well- known continental cracks, such as Jacquelin, Rutt, Van der Born, Mayer, Eros. F4rrarie, Mondt, and the ex-amateur Hinz. Callaghan and Barden worthily ' upheld the honour of Old England, Callagham, benefited from his tub-track training, rode splendidly, and divided the honours with Rutt and Meyer. THE NEW RUSSIAN AMBASSADOR. It has been an open secret in diplomatic circles for the past two years, that when Baron de Staal resigned his post of Russian Ambassador to the Court of St. 'James's, he would be succeeded by Count Beckendorff, the Russian Minister at Copenhagen, and no choice could be more popular or more suitable. In his official cnacity at Copenhagen he has frequently come into contact with our King and Queen, who are so closely allied to the Czar through the Danish connection: and he has thus often come under the personal notice of both the Czar and King Edward at the same moment, so he cannot be counted entirely a stranger: and he is very pops- hr alrea.;y in royal circles. For identically the same reason it will be remem- bered,Sir Charles Scott, who was , .British Minister at Copenhagen, iv as chosen to fill the post of British Amb sea- dor to the Court of St. Petersburg in 189,4, when Sir Nicholas O'Conot was sent to Constan- tinople : and this nouNT BECKSITDOBFF experiment ha s met with con- siderable success. Copenhagen is always a strong link between the two royal families, which cannot be broken by political differences, however great : and the Ministers to the Court of Denmark are always selected with a view to learning the great diplo- matic lesson of Anglo-Russian friendship trom the practical example of the crowned heads of the two nations. Count Beckendorff, prior to his appointment to Copenhagen, had filled many minor diplomatic posts in the course of his training and had risen to special favour with the Czar, who selected him to succeed the 'late Count Muravieff in Denmark in MI. He is a !Russian Conneillor of Stato and a Master of the Court, and has an hereditary with Russian diplomacy in England through tar. grand-aunt, the Princess Lieven, who was, faas.ous as the Madame Novikoff of her day. His appoint- ment cannot fail to add tO the Anglo-Russian fetent4 aordia2s.

"Lady Huntworth's Experiment."

In aid of the funds of the N.S.P.C.C., a fourth per- formance of this comedy was given in the Royal Court Theatre on Saturday evening by the members of the Dramatic Society. There was a good attendance, the prices of admission having been reduced. The play was again presented in excellent style, and gave the greatest pleasure to the audience.. The Disaster at Barton Locks.

The° large lock at Barton has been repaired and the sunken tug removed. The work was completed during Sunday night, and traffic through that lock was re- sumed on Monday. Traffic has been passing through the smaller lock without any interruption. Band of Hope Work in Lancashire and Cheshire.

A meeting of the Executive of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Upidn was held in St. Paul's School, Ramsbdttom on Saturday afternoon. Mr. J. Walkdeti, of Glossop, presided, and representatives were present from 54 towns in Lancashire and Cheshire. Reports were presented showing that the day school lecturers to the Counties Union had given 767 lectures in elementary day schools from January Ist until November 30th. A discussion took place upon a scheme for raising £15,000 with the object of carrying on scientific temperance teaching in day schools' for the next five years and to provide for the erection of suitable offices in Deansa°ate, Manchester, for the Union's head- quarters. Towards this sum it was reported that the Union had received personal promises amounting to nearly £3OO, in addition to the promises made on behalf of the Associated Band of Hope Unions and Societies. It was mentioned that the Board of Trade had granted a charter of incorporation to the Union, unto which all properties of the Union which may and have been required,will for all time be devoted to Band of Hope purposes. It was decided that the anrual meeting of the Union be held on February 14th in Manchester. •

COMMERCIAL FAILURES.—ACCOrding to 'Kemp. Mercantile Gazette," the number of New Bankruptcy Proceedings in England and Wales gazetted during the week ending December 13th, was 76. The number in th corresponding week of last year was 80, showing an increase of 4, being a net decrease in 1902,t0 date, of 13, AN ENTERPRISING GLOVER.—There has just been published an interesting illustrated booklet.on "The Glove of the Period and How it is made :—A Tour through the great glove factories of France, Belgium, Saxony and Bohemia," by Mr. Henry Miles, C.C., of Liverpool, head of the well-known firm of Henry Miles and Co., milliners, glovers and fancy drapers, of Church- street and Williamson-street, Liverpool. During Septem- ber and October last, Mr. Miles travelled from two to three thousand miles on the Continent in search of novelties for his customers and this booklet is the result of his visit to the great glove houses of the Con- tinent. Mr. Miles wields a facile pen and gives an interesting account of the different processes Of manu- facturing suede and kid gloves. The work is enhanced by a number of illustrations showing the glove opera- tives at work. The last half-dozen pages of the booklet are occupied by the history and associations of gloves generally. Copies of the booklet can be had free on application to Henry Miles and Co.

BROUGHTON RANGERS v. BATLEY. Five thousand spectators were present at this match at Wheater's Field, Broughton. The game was ex- tremely fast, and ultimately Batley took up a strong aggressive position, with the result that Oakland secured from the pack, and scored a clever try near the posts. Davies easily placed a goal. Afterwards the home side had the best of matters, despite the visitors' line forward play, and the result was—Broughton Rangers 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points), Batley 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).

div.head: Death of Ex-Inspector Cox.
div.p: Death of Ex-Inspector Cox.

We regret to announce the death of Ex-laspector Cox, who for twentv-six and a half years was a mem- ber of the Warrington Police Force. The deceased gentleman, who was fifty-six years of age gassed away very suddenly in the garden at his residence Richmond Villas, Brooks Estate, Monmouth, about noon On Monday. He was held in great respect in Warrington, and the news of his death will be received with general regiet. He retired from the police force oar years ago.

ANOTHER safeguard to Dishonouring the the public liberties hits House of Commons. gone by the Board. By a series of most amazing tricks—we can find no other word that is so accurately descriptive—the House of L >rds has been taught how it may safely alter the terms of a money Bill without invading the privileges of the House of Commons. It: is thus provided with a new and ready weapon by which, lilt had then existed, it would have been able to prevent Mr.GLAnsrowe's repeal of the Paper Duties,and threughwhieh it will in future become the!master of the House of Commons to an extent hitherto undreamed of. What took place in the House of Commons on Tuesday makes it fairly clear that the PRIME MINISTER either Suggested or assented to the BISHOP of MANCHESTER'S House of Lords' amendment, of which fact it is probable that the DUKE of Devommue, who protested against the amendment, was kept in ignorance. For what has been, the course of events? When the Education Bill gets to the House of Lords it is discovered that there is still one respect in which the ratepayer may be further fleeced, and one more small burden of which the voluntary subscriber may be retie% ed. The BISHOP of MAN- CHESTER carries an amendment by which the local authorities, instead of the school managers, are made responsible for wear and tear in what are now called not " voluntary " but " unprovided " schools. This it is at once pointed out is going be- yond the limits of the power possessed by the House of Lords. It is an invasion of the privileges of the House of Commons. Some of the Lords say" Pooh, pooh," or something of that sort. But the wiser of more cautious peers do not wish to risk a collision with the Lower Chamber, or even to come under the reproof of Mr. SPEAKER. Teen the Dolce of NORFOLK comes to the rescue. He succeeds in adding words to the BisHor of Man- chester's amendment which make it self-contradic- tory and ridiculous, but which deprive it of the element of breach of privilege. This was done, it seems, after a conference with Mr. BALFOUR for the time being the especial guardian, af tar the Speaker of the House of Commons. And we can now see why that conference was considered to be necessary, and what-was arranged thereat. It was the PRIME IVlrsairren's plain duty take •steps to pincers the elimination of the Bishop Of MANCHESTER'S amendment. He was bound to this course as well by honour and loyalty to colleague t as by constitutional considerations. The amendment had been opposed in the House of Lords on behalf of the Government. The DUKE of DEVONSHIRE had manfully declined to accept or to approve it. Ma. BALFOUR was expected to do the same in the House of Commons if the oppor- tunity should arise. But what appeared on the papers ofithe House on Tuesday was a proposal not to refuse the Burro? of MAncsnoTea's amendment, but to get rid of the Duna of NORFOLK'S addition to it. "The words inverted in brackets and under- lined," it was said," are proposed to be omitted in the Commons." These words were those added at Doc.z of NORFOLK, and the instance of the they served the purpose—the very mean and idis• honest purpose we are bound to say—of enabling the BISHOPS' amendment to get safely past the Speaker. Mr. GULLY ruled on Tuesday that, bad the amendment gone before the CM:llmoms in it original form, it would ha've been a breach of the' privileges of the House; but that the Dime of NORFOLK'S addition, ridiculous as it might be derived it of that character, since it no longer was a charge on public funds. The amendment might under these circumstances be discussed en its merits. Is an attack on the priiileges of the elected representatives of the people it would have been opposed even by many of the supporters of the Govern ment, for the Constitutional

div.p: party actually does contain some constitu- tionalists. However, the DUKE of NORFOLK'S far from dainty device did the work for which it was designed, and Mr BALFOUR revealed himself in the character of a PRIME IVIINisrEa who has circum- vented the House of Commons in order to deprive it of one of its most cherished rights. For let it be clearly understood what the Peers have Acme with this Bill they may cl,) with any other. The ques- tion of how to interfere with a Money Bill to parts' of which they object, will no longer present any difficulties to them. Tkey will make an essential change and then add some stupid words which , will deprive it of the character of a breach of the , Commons' privilege. Thus, for exatnple,they may remodel the Budget and add such words as" pro- vided that these proposals shall have no effect on the revenue." Such phrases as these having deprived the Speaker of his power to sustain the privileges:of the House eau then be dropped as on this occasion, and the Lords will have gained a power for which they have contended spas- modically and vainly for centuries past.

div.head: POISONING MYSTERY. -- Startling Evidence against Chapman.
div.p: THE POISONING MYSTERY. -- Startling Evidence against Chapman.
Another DT in the Case.

A large crowd on Wednesday attended Southwark Police Court, when further evidence was given against George Chapmamuntil recently landlord of the Crown public house, Borough High-street, who is charged with the murder of his barmaid. Maud Marsh. At the last hearing. Dr, Steven,son gave his opinion that death was due to poisoning by antimony,and said his analysis of the various organs showed that they contained seven grains of metallic antimony (20 glains of tarter emetic). A fatal dose of tartar emetic would be 15 grains' - Mr. William Davidson, a retired chemist, told how he was in business at High-street, Hastings, in 1897. Mr. • Davidson explained that he knew prisoner as a barber in George-street, Hastings, in 1897. He remembered Chap- man asking if he could purchase tartar emetic, °and a few days after witness sold him sonic. Tt was put in a bottle and labelled. A label was handed to witness, which bore his writing, but he could not say whether it was the label placed on the bottle he sold Chapman. The labelsbore the instimetions :—" One-sixth of a grain to a quarter of a grain. To be used with caution." Mr. Davidson said he often had conversations with Chapman about medical books, and he was led to believe he anderstood medicine. Two books were handed to wit- ness, the titles of which did not transpire, but one of which witness described as a "general recipe" book. He identified them as having been sold by him to Chapman. , Miss Florence Raynor, a tall, good-looking girl, said ' that about the beginning of June She was at work close to the Crown, and used to go into the bar and talk to Mr. and Mrs. Chapman. One Saturday she mentioned to Chapman that she had been a barmaid, and he asked her to come and work for him. She went in on the following Monday. After she had been there a short time Chapman kissed her several times, and asked her if , she would go to America with him. "No, you have got your wife downstairs, you don't want me,' replied Miss Raynor; and Chapman said, "I could giveher that (snapping his fingers) and she would not be any more." Chapman then suggested to her that she should go over to America and he would follow, when he had sold his business. When she went to the Crown first, Mrs. Chapman was quite well, but the first week in July she fell ill. Chap- man used to kiss witness at meals when Mrs. Chapman was not there, and he was always nice to her. At this point in her evidence, Miss Raynor, who had been keeping her eyes fixed on Chapman, fainted, and , had to be carried out of court. She returned after a short time, and said that after leaving the Crown he wont to the Fortescue Arms, Peckham, and one day, while in the bar, Chapman came in. She asked him how Mrs. Chapman was, and he replied that she was in the hospital, and had been three weeks. Chapman added, "If you had not been such a fool you would have been in: the Crown now." Miss Raynor had not seam Chapman since. Mr. Sydney (Chapman's solicitor) : Did you ever ' complain to anyone about Chapman kissing you? Witness : Not to anyone. You left the Crown under unpleasant circumstances. You were drunk, were you not Witness indignantly denied that she was drunk. The drink he gave her made her bad. • lint you were charged here with being drunk ? Witness admitted this, but said that was on a Wednes- day morning, and she left the Crown on the Monday. On the Wednesday morning she went to the Crown to obtain a reference, and Chapman pushed her out of the house, saying she was drunk, and hadbetter comewhen she was sober. • 4 formal remand was granted for a week.

div.head: VERDICT OF MURDER AGAINST CHAPMAN.
div.p: VERDICT OF MURDER AGAINST CHAPMAN.

-- After an adjournment of over three weeks, Dr. Waldo, the Southwark Coroner, on Thursday resumed his in- quiry into the death of Maud Marsh. Detective-Inspector Godley gave a list of the things he found at the "Crown." There were several bottles and powders, and a number of medical works. He found in one of the books the label which was produced at the police court bearing the inscription "one-sixth of a grain to a quarter of a grain. To be used with cau- tion." Dr. Freiburger and Dr. Stevenson gave evidence as to the examination of the stomach. The latter repeated evidence given at the police court as to the presence of i antimony n every organ. He found altogether 2012 grains of tartar emetic, Fifteen grains was the average fatal dose. Miss Marsh, in his opinion, died from antimony poisoning. , After other evidence the jury found that death was due tonntimony poison, administered by Chapman, and he was committed for trial on the capital charge.,

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday at Dutton. Present—Messrs J. Knowles (in the chair), E. Clarke, J. Mclntyre, J. Stokes, T. Darlington, T. Baxter, C. E. Linaker, T. Lewis, T. Wright, H. Mawdsley, G. Pilling, J. Edwards, J. Spruce, R. Billington, J. Mountield, T. Antwiss, with G. E. Ash- ton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (Medical Officer of Health), J. Farrington (Inspector), W. Diggle and J. Swinton (surveyors). • THE RUNCORN WATER. . _

A lengthy resume of the negotiations referring to the dispute with the 14incorn Urban Council as to the conditions of the wategsupplied by them to Halton and Weston was submitted by the Clerk. This included extracts from the minute books of the Halton, Weston, I and Rural Council's from October 1901 to the present time, copies of bacteriological and chemical analysis I taken at various periods, and extracts from the Medical , officer's reports (all of which were unsatisfactory in tone), and concluded with the correspondence with the Runcorn Urban District Council, referring to the dis- tinctly .favourable analysis recently obtained from Professor Boyce. This correspondence has already been dealt with in our reports of the Urban District Council and Halton Parochial Committee meetings. The summary also contained reference to analysis taken on behalf of the Runcorn Urban District Council, both bacteriological and chemical, which were consistently satisfactocy. j The Clerk said they had thus seen that while the analysts of the Rural District Council condemned the water as bad, those of the Urban Council said it was good. Mr- Wright said that as there seemed to be consider- able difference between the analysts, zinc' the matter affected the two townships considerably he moved that a committee be appointed to investigate the question thoroughly, consisting of the Chairman and the Vice- Chairman of the Council, with Messrs. Wright, Stokes, Guest, Linaker, the Clerk and the Medical • Officer of Health. Mr. J. Spruce seconded. Mr. Linakor: It is is very , serious matter to the Urban Council and the two townships. ,

The resolution was passed. DAMAGING A ROADWAY. Mr. Baxter drew attention to the fact that on the road below Hill Cliff Chapel the road was being terribly cut up by carters who were excavating on an adjoining field.
The Surveyor said he had complained to Mr. Miller, the contractor about he damage who promised to attend to the matter. - - -
The Clerk said he could be held responsible for the damage and a claim could be made and asked to be furnished with particulars. Mr. Baxter promised to get the necessary informa- tion.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

On the whole the match on Saturday was a very poor one. Theßovers more thanheld their own inthe earlier stages of the game and could they but have maintained the pace,the score could never have been so large. As it was they fell to pieces when every advantage was in their favour. Runcorn unquestionably won by sheer good. play there being a capital understanding between the front rank and the rear division. At forward the Linnets were rather outplayed but the Rovers' backs did not, in the least, avail themselves of the opportunities given them. Each of the home team shone to advan- tage and it would be invidious to make comparisons.

div.head: NEWTON DOCTOR'S ACTION.
div.p: NEWTON DOCTOR'S ACTION.
Order for Administration of an Estate.

An unusual action—we believe the first of its kind which has been heard at Warrington for many years— Came before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., at the Warrington County Court on Thursday. Des. John Webb Watkins,and Harold Ernest Watkins' New- ton, took proceedings against Gustave Fairall, Eagles Hotel, Ladbroke Grove, London W., the executor of Mary Ann Gorse deceased, either to obtain payment of £23 16s, being the amount of plaintiffs' account against Mary Ann Gorse for medicinis and medical attendance, or failing that, an order to have the estate of Mary Ann Gorse administered. Mr. E. A. White represented the plaintiffs, and Mr. H. J. Longton defended. Mr. White said he understood there was no question• as to the amount'of the claim. Mary Ann Gorse died at the " Oak Tree" Hotel, Neivton, on June 9th, 1901. By her will, after directing payments, debts, funeral and other expenses, she bequeathed the goodwill, stock, licence, fittings, furniture and effects in connection with the business carried on at the " Oak Tree' Hotel," Itogether with the business premises to her daughter, Louisa Martha, on certain conditions. The will NNW proved on June 17th, and on August Bth the licence was transferred to the daughter, who took possession of the Ipremises, stock, furniture, and goodwill, and carried on ' the business. Subsequently she was married to a Mr. Toft, and the licence was transferred in her married name. I Mr. Longton said he did not admit that Mr. Toft - !entered into possession 1 Continuing, Mr. White stated that on July 15th, 1902, his firm wrote to the executor of the late Mrs. Gorse— not then knowing who the executor was, applying for payment of the account of the plaintiffs. On July 23rd Mr. Longton telephoned to him (Mr. White) and said he would schedule plaintiffs' as creditors and keep him (Mr. White) informed as to the position of matters. On August 7th Mr. Longton wrote stating that the amount realized by a sale of the fittings. &c., was very small and would leave nothing whatever for the unpaid creditors. On the 3rd of November, baying been informed that the defendant was the executor, his (Mr. White's) firm wrote to him stating that they had been instructed to insti- tute legal proceedings for the :recovery of the account unless it was paid within a certain time. A reply was received from the defendant to the effect that he was given to understand that the account had been paid, and he was writing to his niece and to Mr Langton on the subject. -Nothing further having been heard the case was entered into Court. On the 16th instant Mr. Long- ton 'wrote stating ,that the bills Ltc, with reference to the hotel were in his hands and clearly, showed, that there was nothing left for theplaintiffs. The dpcuments were opened for the,inspection of the xaintiffs or his solicitors.. The following day he (Mr. White) attended at Mr. Longton's office to inspect them. He found that the assets which had beim sworn by the executor at the death tote £266 were now stated to have produced only .£l4B is. sd. The household goods veined at £BO at the date of the 'death were stated to have realized only £62 is. sd. The stock-in-trade was taken over by Mrs. Toft at the executors' valuation of £25, and the goodl will of the business which had been valued at £lOO by the executor at the time of Mrs. Gorse's death was new I stated to be worth nothing. • Considerable argument ensued with reference to the good will. Mr. Longton contending that there was no good will because the hotel was a tied house and the 1 brewers declined to recognized the good-will. Mr. White submitted that whatever view the brewers took of the matter there was the value of the house to 1 an incoming tenant. His Honour said he had considerable experience in licensing matters, and what ever views the brewers took of them there was in some cases, if not a good-will in the strictly legal sense of the Word, something in the nature of a good-will usually paid by the, incoming tenant. Mr. White also contended that the executors had allowed Mrs. Toft to take possession of the whole estate without making any provision for the payment of debts, and he was therefore chargeable with the value of the estate at the time Mrs. Toft took it over, plus four per cent. interest. It would be very difficult to fine the exact value, but defendant should at least be charged with his own estimate of £266. if defendant had not allowed Mrs. Toft to take possession he had carried on the business inher name and was equally liable. His Honour said that on the 'facts admitted by Dr. Longton an administration order could not be escaped. He made an order for the Registrar to take an account of the personal estate, debts, and funeral expenses. to make inquiry whether Mrs. Toft took possession of the assets as alleged, also to make inquiry whether the defendant improperly'carried onthe trade, and to certify the result to the Court before March 19th.
