div.head: BACHELORS BILL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BACHELORS BILL AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening at the Guild Hall, one of the most fashionable balls held for many years was cele- brated. Over fifty couples, consisting of the elite of Runcorn were present and the proceedings were a com- plete success. The ball was inaugurated by the bachelors of the town. At the conclusion of the proceedings a vote of thanks was passed to the committee on the pro- position of Mr. Imison. Mr. Lawrenson M.A.'responded for the committee. The catering, which was done in excellent style, was by Mr. T. Lea of High-street.

div.head: CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS AT EARLESTOWN.,
div.p: CHRISTMAS HOLIDAYS AT EARLESTOWN.,

--- For the Christmas and New Year holidays the Viaduct Works will close on Wednesday night next till Monday morning, and again from the following Wednesday to Monday morning. The Vulcan Foundry closes from Wednesday night to Monday morning, but will not close at the New Year. Messrs.'''. and T. Wears will close on same dates as the Vulcan and will not close for the New Year. •

T.O.G.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGE The weekly meeting of the above washeld on Monday. Bro. T. E. Greening, C.T„ presided Over a fair attend- ance of members. The programme of the evening consisted of impromptu speeches; the arrangements being in the hands of the secretary. Several subjects were brought forward, the most interesting being "Is Earl Grey's scheme of Public House Trust likely to advance the cause of Temperance." The following members spoke: Bros. Singleton, Woods, Newman, Hatton. Williams. The debate was very interesting and it was decided to Adjourn it till next week. An enjoyable and profitable evening was spent.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.

In aid of these schools a sale of work and Christmas tree was held in the Mission Hall,Earlestown, on Satur- day evening. There were altogether seven stalls on which were displayed for sale urticles of a useful and fancy description, together with dowers, toothsome dainties and refreshments. There were two Christmas trees and in order to make the affair more realistic one of the officials acted as Father Christmas, and distri- buted the things from the trees to the youngsters. The sale should have been presided over by Mr. T. Moly- neux, but he was unavoidably absent, and the necessary formalities of opening were performed by the Vicar (Rev. 'ER. Matthews). There was a fair attendance at the opening which was augmented as the day advanced, and the business done was of a satisfactory character. The amount realised was about £2O. SAD BURNING FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN. Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner conducted an inquest at the Town Hall Earlestown on Wednesday, touching the death of Annie Trigg, the 12 months old daughter of William Trigg a brick-setters labourer, of 43, Birch-street, Earlestown. Mary Jane Trigg, mother of deceased, stated that at about half-past three on Thursday afternoon the 11th December she left deceased in arocking chair on the right-hand side of the kitchen fire whilst she was hanging out clothes in the back yard. On returning to the kitchen a few minutes later, she heard the child crying, and hurrying to her, found deceased's clothes on fire, as she sat in the chair, in the exact place where witness had left her before going into the yard. With the aid of a shawl, witness, and a next- door neighbour—Mrs Mannion—put the flames out and employed linseed oil and flour to soothe the child's pain. Dr Gauge was called in and attended the child up to her death which occurred at 4 o'clock on Monday morning. The chair was some distance from the fire and although another child aged three years was in the room, it was asleep both when witness left the room and when she returned. Witness's supposition was, that a spark fell from the fire and set the deceased clothes on fire. She had been a Weakly child since birth. A verdict of ' Accidental Death " was returned. EARLESTOWN HOMING SOCIETY. . .

On Saturday the annual dinner of the above Society was held at the Griffin Hotel, Earlestown. Mr. H. J ! Longton took the chair, and E. Alf Slate% of the Blackbrook (Haydock) Society, was unanimously toted to the vice-chair, support being rendered by Mr. Jackson and Mr Clough (secretary). The Secretary (Mr. T. E. Clough) read the report and balance-sheet,and said :—Mr. president and gentlemen, I beg to lay before you a brief report relative to the business of this society for the year 1902. There have been 27 members, com- pared with 29 last year, and we have convoyed and liberated for them 1,704 birds, as compared with 1,791 last year, 1,741 in 1900, and 1,503 in 1899. We coin- meneed the season with a bank balance of £1 19s. 10d. and after paying all expenses and £lB in club, prizes beside £5 produce Stakes, £7 2s. 6d. in lieu of silver cups, and other specials, we have a debit balance of 5s The chairman moved the adoption of the report and balance-sheet, and it was carried unanimously. During the evening some excellent songs were rendered by Messrs. F. Ogden, Tom Beatty,Haynes,W. Shaw,etc., and Mr. Maudesley gave selections on the gramaphone. Mr. J. Sandiford very kindly. acted as accompanist.— The prizes were all paid out ID Cheques, the winners of cups preferring money to silver plate:.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY' AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY' AT EARLESTOWN.

The recent level crossing fatality at Earlestown appealed very strongly to the jury at the inquest. They evidently considered the spot an exceptionally dan- gerous one, by reason of its position: Trains approach- ing it from one direction come down an incline, and any- one intending to cross the linecan do so without let er hindrance, because of the unguarded state of the cross- ing. They must be very wary though, and before cross- ing it is quite necessary that pedestrians should keep a careful look out, owing to the projecting bank hiding the approach• of trains proceeding to Warrington, or it might not be very pleasant for them.. Consequently the jury added a recommendation that the gate should be' kept locked and that the Railway Company should put a bridge over the crossing. If theylcould close it alto- gether it would be better.

Another. point which appealed to the jury who were empanelled for the drowning of a woman. %Alen found the woman could not be recognised,and she was removed to the mortuary at the cemetery. This meant that any member of the jury living in Earlestown had probably to walk a mile and a half to the mortuary in order to view the body. The wisdom of placing this receptacle for unknown dead bodies here has often been question- ed, but it would be hard to find a more isolated place. Earlestown is year by year more populated, and the residents might not relish the establishment of a mortu- arybin their midst. Still, it is a hardship on a jury to have to walk to the bottom end of the cemetery to view a body.

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL.

The 'wind-up OithWS'eS;i:CM-1;;;--h-eld on Tuesday evening, the proceedings taking the form of a social. There was a very good gathering, several local artistes giving selections. CAMDEN SALE OF WORK.

In connection with the Camden Sunday school a sale of work and Christmas tree was opened on Thursday afternoon by Mr. J. Povah. There was a brisk business done during the afternoon and evening,the proceeds of which will be devoted to the cleaning and decorating of the Sunday school. THE LIBRARY AND READING Room. _ _

At the monthly meeting of the Library Committee on Tuesday, it was resolved to close the lending depart- ments on Christmas Day, Boxing Day, New Year's Day and the day following and to open the reading room on Boxing Day and New Year's Day.

CAMDEN MISSIONARY MEETING. The annual missionary meeting was held at Camden on Tuesday Mr. R. H. Posnett taking the place of Mr. Bosten who could not attend. Mr. Anders read the report which showed a decrease of £8 18s. 7d. The chairman appealed for a good sum to make up the de- ficiency and remarked that the chairman who should have been present had sent a note.—Other speakers addressed the meeting which was closed in the usual manlier.

div.head: HALTON-ROAD FOREIGN MISSION.
div.p: HALTON-ROAD FOREIGN MISSION.

The above mission took the form of a conversazione held on Saturday evening at the Halton-road Church. The Rev. W. T. C. Coppin and the Rev. J. B. Foster,with several young men gave representations of Oriental customs illustrating Bible scenes and passages. At Camden Church on Sunday the mission services were held, Mr. H. Dodd preaching in the morning and the Rev. W T. C. Coppin in the evening. .
SERIOUS DAMAGE TO __THE RUNCORN TRANSPORTER
BRIDGE.

On Tuesday night a steamer, name unknown. described as about a thousand tons, collided with the stage erected round the cylinders in the Ship Canal which are to form the foundation of the Transporter Bridge across the Mersey. The ship continued her voyage apparently uninjured, but the staging appeared wrecked, and a pile leans over the canal at an angle of about 45 degrees. Fortunately no men were on the job at the time. The damage is stated to be very heavy, and will delay the contractors considerably. ' VICTORIA -ROAD BOARD SCHOOL.

The annual concert 'in connection with the above schools was given on Monday and Wednesday evenings in the Drill Hall, Runcorn. 14,T the boys of the schools. A very interesting programme was submitted on both occasions, the principal feature being the comic operetta entitled "The Pied Piper of Hamelin." The boys played their parta with admirablespirit, and had evidently been carefully trained. At the conclusion of the concert, Mr. James Pritchard; chairman of the School Board,proposed a vote of thanks to the following for assistance rendered in various directiops : Messrs. H. Caddick, A Abel, F. W. Hutton, J. Beck, J. Pritchard, and the committee of St. John's Sunday School, C. Handley. T. Bowyer, J Pritchard, W. Bylleld, H. Branch, Captain Ashton, and the officers of the local Volunteers, Mr. Moulton, and the teachers. Mr. W. Handley seconded and the motion was carried.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday at Dutton. Present :—Messrs. A. J.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday at Dutton. Present :—Messrs. A. J.
RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A CORRESPONDENT].

At present the Rural Council are considering a very important proposal of Mr. Linaker. The report of the committee appointed to consider the question should have been read at the last ,meeting, but, evidently; no unanimous result was arrived at. Mr. Linaker's pro-. posal really amounts to this: that the Rural Council shall meet monthly instead of fortnightly as hitherto. The probability is that this meeting will have to beheld in a week between the Guardians' meetings which means,that members will have to meet three times in the month instead of twice. Mr. Linaker's argument appears to be that the Council bnsiness is so important that sufficient time cannot be devoted to it so long as the Guardians take until two o'clock to finish their meeting. It is to be hoped that this motion will be strenuously resisted by the District Councillors. At the present time to attend the Guardian meeting a whole day has, of necessity, to be sacrificed; and while the men are on the spot the Council business might just as well be proceeded with, without sacrificing another business day on the altar of public business.

It will be a most satisfactory thing for everybody concerned if the Guardians can persuade the War Office to pay, some of the local reservists' pensions weekly instead of quarterly. It is to be feared that there are too many cases in the district where men draw their quarterly pension and waste it inside the seven days, spending the rest of the quarter in a semi-starved condition. It will be a booTi and a blessing to the wives and children of such men if the pensions be made pay- able in small weekly amounts.

When experts differ who'shall decide? This was the plaintive cry of Mr. Wright respecting the quality of Runcorn water. It is certainly a most singular fact that the experts employed by the District Council have, unhesitatingly, pronounced the water to be bad, while the experts of the Urban Council have pronounced it to be good. The Rural Council have appointed a Com- mittee to investigate the matter thoroughly, and the probability is that eventually Somerset House will be called in to decide the question.

div.p: WARRINGTON.
A Daring_ Barglary.---Hams, Tobacco, and
Cash Stolen.

The premises of Messrs. Kay and Cowdell, provision dealers, Forster-street, were the seem, of a daring burglary between twelve and one o'clock on Thursday morning. It appears that a woman who lives opposite the shop was bolting the door of her house, when she saw several men leaving the shop by the front door carrying a hani under each arm. She gave information to Seargeant Evans and another con-stable, who happened to be in the vicinity, and it was found that the three locks and the bar on the door had been wrenched off. The thieves succeeded in carrying away twenty-for harns;.and also 2.51 h. of tobacco, half a flitch' of bacon and 4s. in money. The total valite of the Spoils is about £25. The depredators had lighted the shop gas and did not turn it Out when they left. The police are making inquiries. , H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE Tom() is the KING OF TONICS.-63,,SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. TRY A PAIR of ALP TAYLOR'S Kangaroo Boots. Better now than ever.—Advt. A Farmer's Claim for Cutting Corn.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, be- fore His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., an action was heard in which John Owen, of Woodhouse . Farm, Haydock, claimed £2 is. 6d. from William ; Bryan, of Pennington-lane Farm, Burtonwood, the I price of cutting 31 acres, of corn.—Mr. Unsworth re- presented the plaintiff and iffr. Browne the defendant. In stating the case, Mr. Unsworth stated that the de- fendant's son asked Mr.'critchley, the manager of. the plaintiff's farm if he would cut his corn with the plain- tiff's machine and self binder. After a consultation with the 'plaintiff, Mr. Critchley informed the defend- ant that the plaintiff would ,cut the corn for him at 12s. 6d. per Cheshire acre, thb defendant also to pay for the string used in the binding. The corn was cut in I} days but the ;defendant now disputed the account. Evidence was given in support of the plain- tiff's case ,by William Critchley and John Owen bear- ing out M. Unsworth's statement. William Cawley, burleynian, Haydock, said he considered 12s. 6d: per Cheshire acre a cheap rate for cutting corn. He had got more than that amount himself. In cross-examination, witness said he had never heard of corn being cut at 12s. 6d. per day with a machine and self-binder.—For the defence, Mr. Browne contended that the agreement was for 12s. 6d. per day, plus the cost of the string. The defendant had paid 335. into Court, which he considered was the amount agreed upon.—After , evidenca had been given by William Bryan, his Honour said the weight of evidence was on the side of the plaintiff, and he gave judgment for the plaintiff with I costs.

THE DOCTOR'S ENEM Y.—A . pair of ALF TAYLOR'S Wonderful Boots.—Advt.. A Cattle Dealer Found Drowned. Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, conducted an inquest at the 'Warrington olice Station on Monday afternoon relative to the death of Patrick Ginick, aged 60, a, cattle dealer, residing in West-street, whose body was recovered from the Mersey behind Wilders- pool Causeway on Saturday morning.—Evidence of identification was given by Catherine Gillick, deceased's wife, who lived apart from.hint—A boy named Charles Appleby; Who resides at 59, Wilders- pool-road,. said he saiw the dedeased at nine O'clock on Friday night. He was under the influence of drink, and was going in the, direction, of the river.—ln answer to Mr. Browne, witness said there was another man with. deceased, but witness did not recognise him. —Police-constable Hamblen stated that at a quarter- past ten on Satnrday, morning he was on duty in Wilderspool-road; when he was informed that a body was floating in the river. He. obtained grappling irons land got the body out of the water. It was conveyed to t.lw mortuary.—Detective Barlow, coroner's officer, said were no marks of violence on the body. He :round the possession of the deceased, a watch and chain; 01d., sonic tobacco, and several papers, includ- ing one or two The watch had stopped at ten minutes to eleven. The deceased had been drink- ing during the last month, and on the, night in question he had been refused drink at the Bridge Inn—The jury returned a verdict of " Fouyd drowned."

Concert at Latchford. • Alarge audience assembled in the Parish loom, Latchford, on 'Monday evening, When a concert in aid of Christ 'Church enfargemmt • fund was held: The event was a 'complete success, and it is expected that , the proeeeds will almost if not entirely extinguish the small debt which existed in connection with the recent . enlargement of the Church. The Vicar (Rev. F. A. . Screetm.) presided, and cordially thanked the Corona- tion Committee, by whom the concert • had been „pro 7 'noted. An interesting programme had been arranged, and the ' efforts of the artistes who gave their services, were fully appreciated. The opening item was a well executed' pianoforte due by M T. L. Fry and Miss Annie Fry, 'which was well received. The vocalists were Miss Pierpoint,`Miss B. Eckendey, Mr. W. Booth, am! Mr. L. Arddand all of whom .acquitted themselves very creditably. Miss Pierpoint was heartily ern:ored for an expressive in- terpretation, " 0 dry those tears," and later on fihe sang " Winter" very eff4ctively. Miis Eckersler was very successful, having the honour of a recall for each of her songs--" There is a Land" and "All in the hush of Twilight." Mr. W. Booth was heard to advan- tage in "The sailor's Grave" and "The parting of the Ways." Mr. L. Auldaud gave a spirited' ren- dering ,of " The Yeoman's Wedding" and in response to. a vigorous encore sang "Will o'th' Wisp. " He also gave " The young loyalist" with success. Mr. A. Bennett contributed two . violin .solos with taste and skill, and Miss M. Fain:lough was recalled for a pianoforte solo. One of the most enjoyable items •of the evening was a dramatic Sketch ‘`ln two minds" by the Misses Broadbent, Which was admirably presented, and gave the greatest pleasure to the audience. The humorous element was in the capable hands of Mr. H. Hallard who fully maintained his: high reputations. His sketches created unbounded mirth,and encores were freely'. accorded. The duties of accompanist were efficiently discharged by Mr. 'l'. L. Fry.

Alderman SUTTON pointed out that there were two motions of a similar nature upon the paper, and if they decided which should be taken into consideration it would save much time and avoid the necessity of having the same discussion over again. Councillor PEACOCK claimed that his motion should be considered because it gave a better opportunityof carrying out the second if it was passed, than if the other were brought forward and passed in the place of it. Alderman SuTrox : It is just to save time. Councillor TINNION: Time's no object. Alderman HEATON: Oh, let's go on; it's only Tuesday night yet. (Laughter). The CHAIRMAN: I think we had better hear what Councillor Peacock has to say. Councillor PEACOCK then proposed his motion which was couched in the following terms :—"That an inquiry be held into,and respecting the various charges made by certain members of the Conncil,who allege that irre- gularities have been committed by this Council from November Ist 1897, to November Ist, 1902, and that the expenses of such inquiry be defrayed out of the rates." He claimed to bring in that motion he said, because he had suffered somewhat by the false and mis- leading statements that had been made against him by a member of that Council—he referred to Councillor Pemberton—who accused him of trading with the Cor- poration, and who had even gone so far as to serve a notice personally upon him threatening proceedings. But like a great number of other vague and untruthful statements that had been made, he evidently found out before it was too late that he had no case, and, there- fore,let it drop. He had not had the moral courage to put him(Councillor Peacock)right in the public estimation. This he called a most unmanly proceeding,and one which every self-respectingEngi ishman wouldresent.(Hear,hea r) The details and extent of the inquiry and the question of who should constitute that tribunal,could very well be arranged by the Council resolving itself into com- mittee, and giving the matter careful consideration; or if it was thought desirable a special Council meeting could be held. These were details which could be dealt with by the Council as a whole after the motion had

Are we here to air our griev..._ all that again. The DEPUTY-MAYOR: What are you in committee for,if not for free discussion? Councillor WILKINSON: He is airing his grievances. Councillor PEACOCK: We are here to defend our- selves. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WILKINSON: He has no right to go over all that again. Might he point out that they were not "going over this again?" They had not before had a chance. This was their Parr Hall. (Laughter.) This was his opportunity to lay before the people of Warrington something like a case, and he, for one, was not going to miss that op- portunity. He was sure that he of ,all men had nothing to fear from an inquiry. What had been investigated by one of his Majesty's courts could not be re-investi- gated by any other tribunal. Therefore he was a perfectly impartial and unprejudiced person. He would only say a few words about it. Reviewing the situa- tion, a good many people had said they had made a great mistake that they did not agree to an inquiry before. He was prepared on the whole to agree with them that that was a mistake,but it was a mistake foun- ded on a misunderstanding of the view which was taken in the town of the charges that had been made. The legality of what had been done by certain members had never been questioned. Reposing on that legality they had said "These gentlemen are knocking their heads against a stone wall. What they will have to do is to go to Parliament and alter this sort ot thing, and 'see that ally member of a limited liabilitycompany who was also a member of a Council should not allow his com- pany to tender to the Corporation for any tender the Corporation may have to bestow." Those who had read the debates of Parliament at the time when this excep- tion in favour of limited liability companies was passed would see that it was not overlooked; and the exception had been made for the reason that it was absolutely impossible to carry on the trade of a town if the mem- bers of limited liability companies were precluded from contracting with the dorpomtion. (Hear,hear.) Their friends at the Parr Hall—he did not want to say a hard word about them ; he was quite content to rely on the strength of his case—their friends had had some inkling of this, for very early they began to discover that it was not sufficient to point out that -srtatin members were trmling as members of limited

been carried. They would be committing a very grave mistake if they went beyond just passing the motion that night. The general details of the inquiry required careful consideration, not by a single individual, but by the whole Council. He thought that it would be very indiscreet for that Council to elect two of the judges from the ranks of the non-traders so called, when, as they were already aware, some of its members were steepled in prejudice against the Council almost as a whole. No, if that inquiry was to be final and effective the man or men who would constitute the tribunal must be absolutely above suspicion, free from party influence and local prejudiee ; a tribunal which would have the entire confidence of the ratepayers and be above all criticism. (Hear, hear.) Tf this was done he ventured to think that the members of that Council, all of whom he believed to be honourable men, would come out of the ordeal no worse for the inquiry. (Hear, hear.) He hoped his motion would be carried, as it would come with better grace if the Council showed that it had nothing to fear and did not budge an inquiry. (Hear, hear). Councillor ELLISON, in seconding the motion, said he did so because it did not bind them as to how the inquiry should be conducted. If they were to have an inquiry it ought to be an independent inquiry. He was quite in favour of such an inquiry, and he believed it would clear the air. (Hear, hear.) div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING. THE INQUIRY GRANTED. Town Council's Unanimous Vote.
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING. THE INQUIRY GRANTED. Town Council's Unanimous Vote.
LIVELY PROCEEDINGS IN COMMITTEE. Misrepresentations set Right.

.Ihe said he thought that irregular would rather be I'legal trading. What was the use of inquiring into trading that was lega 1? A good deal of legal actions might be immoral, and he was in sympathy with the agitation to that extent, and he had done what he could to stop what was called immoral 'trading. Where he differed with the Non-Trading Committee was the manner in which they had gone; about their work so as to cause so much ill- feeling. It was their methods which had given rise to all this. To discuss the matter so, far as legal trading was cancerned was a waste of time. Any judge would refuse to inquire into cases of legal trading. (Hear hear.) Councillor DODDS : That is the point. ALDERMAN ROBERTS' RESIGNATION.

Alderman MONKS continuing, said that what they I wanted was the public opinion which would make it impossible for a man to go on with that kind of legal trading. They had seen this in the resignation of Alderman Roberts. He defied the town and he had had to suffer for it, and there was an end of it so far as he was con- cerned. Did they want to drive out other members who had been guilty of legal trading ?—then go in for their inquiry in this form. Councillor DODDS: That is what we are asking for. Alderman Moss: I think it is a pity that you are going in for any inquiry likely to drive existing mem- bers out of the Council, and thus deprive the town of the services of gentlemen which are still worth retain- ing. The inquiry might be confined to the last two years. Councillor DODDS : I am not going to do anything with my resolution till the air is cleared, but with regard to what Alderman Monks has said, what is the use of an inquiry into legal trading? -What the rate- payers want is an inquiry into the trading by members of the Council, legal or otherwise, direct or indirect. The public say that members of the Council who are members of companies have no right to trade with the Corporation. However legal, it is immoral and ought not to be done.
TRADING AT THE PRESENT TIME. "A SPIRIT OF VINDICTIVENESS."

Alderman SUTTON said the inquiry should extend up to the present time—(hear, hear)—because in that case Mr. Pemberton would feel himself in rather a difficult posi- tion. He Alderman Sutton) was present the other night at one of the committees he attended when a bill was presented connected with a firm in which Councillor Pemberton is interested. Two bills were, in fact, pre- sented for payment, and the Councillor asked the Chair- man whether it would not be better .for him to retire. The Chairman told him he could please himself. He (Alderman Sutton) told him that the best thing for him to do would be to resign—(laughter)—according to the advice Councillor Pemberton had given to everyone.He should have a meeting at the Parr Hall and tell his friends that he was obliged to give up his position be- cause he found he was trading, legally or illegally or in an immoral way, with the Corporation. (Renewed laugh- ter.) Everything the Non-traders could get hold of to the:detriment of the Council had been hionght forward; theirs had been a spirit of vindictiveness, and they had gained their object—and that was to get rid of Alderman Roberts asa member of the Corporation. AN INQUIRY GRANTED, Alderman Bovrou said they wanted one inquiry which would satisfy the Council and the public, i and he sug- gested, therefore, that they vote that an inquiry be held and a committee formed to consider the form of the inquiry. (Hear, hear). Councillor PEACOCK said he should be glad to alter his resolution to read simply "That an inquiry be held." (Hear, hear.) Several members asked if that could be done. _

The TOWN CLERK: You have overlooked the fact that we are in committee, and in committee you can do anything if it is afterwards subjected to the confirma- tion of the Cnuncil when you resume. Councillor PEACOCK: The way the inquiry is to be conducted can be afterwards arranged. Councillor DODDS asked for the rnling of the Town Clerk as to whether his resolution could then come before the Council.

The DEPUTY MAYOR Certainly. Alderman MONKS: If we in committee modify Coun- cillor Peacock's resolution, and resolve ourselves into a meeting of the Council again, can the Council pass the modified resolution?

The TOWN CLERK: No, sir. Alderman IMoNits : For any modification a fresh notice must be given? The DEPUTY MAYOR: Would you reduce your motion to read that an inquiry be held? Couucillor PEACOCK t Yes. .

The DEPTITY'MAYon : Then we will take a vote on it. Councillor PEACOCK : We have been driving at that all along. The resolution of Cotmcillor Peacock, as altered, to read "That an inquiry be held," was then put and carried no one apparently voting against it. The second motion in Councillor Peacock's name was withdrawn, namely, 'That the Mayor be requested to call a town's meeting with the object of ascertain- ing if the ratepayers desire a public inquiry into the charges made by certain ratepayers of the borough, who ' allege tha this coolicii fr, tb., last flveyears have been guilty of certain irregularities which netetbittl,te in- quiry."

div.head: FORM OF THE INQUIRY.
div.p: THE FORM OF THE INQUIRY.

COUNCILLOR DODDS CARRIES HIS MOTION. Alderman- SUTTON: I propose that the form of the inquiry be left to the General Purposes Committee to decide. Councillor TINNTOT : T object. It is only fair that Mr. Dodds should have an opportunity of proposing his resolution. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DODDS moved,—" That a full and exhaus- tive inquiry be forthwith instituted into all the trading with the Corporation for the six years ending the 31st March last by firms in which members of the Council have been, or are partners, or through limited com- panies in which they have been, oFare shareholders, and whether the trading has been done direct or indirect, that is, as contractors or sub-contractors. That the tribunal shall be absolutely independent of this Council as regard its duties, and that it be also empowered to inquire into the question of remuneration for ser- vices rendered by any member of the Town Council. That the tribunal shall have the right to ' inspect all books, documents and vouchers of the Corporation,and to examine any officials,servants or workmen of the Corporation, upon oath or otherwise., That the tribunal shall consist of two members to be appointed by the Municipal Non-Trading Committee, two members to be appointed by the Council, and one member to be elected by the four former, and that the costs of the inquiry be paid by the Corporation." He said : I need not unduly detain the Council in submitting as I now do, the resolution which stands under my name upon page 23 of the agenda paper. The motion is a necessary corollary of the demand of several great meet- ings, held within the last year, and of the results of last month's elections. Those elections have shown that the great majority of the ratepayers have, once for all, made up their minds that any and all trading by mem- bers of the Connell with the Corporation, whether legal or illegal, direct or indirect, through private firms or limited companies' is immoral and must for ever cease. They are also satisfied that for many years past there has been a great deal of this immoral trafficking going on, and they have, therefore, and with no uncertain sound, adopted and endorsed the demand which has been so often made for a full, a comprehensive, and an exhaustive inquiry into all the trading, and all the deal- ings of whatsoever kinehetween members of &Coun- cil and the Corporation of this town during the last six municipal years. The recent elections have brought about in this Council Chamber a condition of things as remarkable as it is unique. For what do we find? Why, that one-tenth part of the Council represents the matured, the declared judgment of the great body of the burgesses of Warrington upon the question of • immoral trading, ' while arrayed against that principle so far as any real, tangible, or substantial sympathy is concerned—that is sympathy backed by any useful act—are the great body of the remaining nine-tenths of the members of the Council. That great majority includes all the aldermen—what or whom they represent or misrepresent on the question now at issue I shall not attempt to guess—it also includes a great number of councillors, who have sought to find salvation under the blessed plea of being opponents of illegal trading, as if there had not been a thousand things in the history of this world that were legal yet highly immoral. I put it to all these gentle- men through von, Mr. Deputy-Mayor, that whatever their credentials may be, they neither represent the senti- ment nor the judgment of Warrington upon the question which has so stirred it during the past twelve or four- teen months. It may be id, "Ah,but you have misrep- resented matters ; • your,ffiave grossly exaggerated the evils ,• you have misled the people!" If that is what you sky. orif that is what you are going to say, then you will vote with me for a full and complete inquiry, so as to prove your contention. If you say, .! Oh, but your own position, though morally right, is legally I doubtful," then I say even if that were so (I believe it

lis not so, lam advised it is not so), but if it were so, that has absolutely nothing to do with the question at issue, which is solely " Will you or will you not grant the inquiry which is demanded?" Why this inquiry is sought, and why I have the serious objections I have to the improper trading and dealings that have been going on in Warrington for so many years past, is not so much because it is wrong in itself, as it assuredly is, but be- cause of its demoralizing affects not only upon mem- bers who have been engaged in it, but also upon the employees of the Corporation who have had from day to day to examine and pass the goods as to quality, quantity and so on, of men neither more nor less than their own employers and masters, with the result that all round the moral sense is blunted, high ideals are undermined, and the tone of public life is lowered and degraded. Let me add that it represents the irreducible minimum of what I and those associated with me will accept. (Hear, hear.) We will not have it reduced in strength in any way. That is our ultimatum. If you can strengthen it in any way I shall be pleased. WHY COUNCILLOR DODDS TOOK UP MUNICIPAL TRADING. A PERSONAL EXPLANATION.

Continuing, Councillor DODDS said: Alderman Monks and Councillor F. R. Roberts are right. The Higginbottom case has brought out the improper nature of this trading. That was what attracted my attention to it, and this answers Councillor F. R. Roberts whexi he says I have been 25 years in Warrington and only just found these things out. As several gentlemen knew I had been the auditor of the Newcastle Corporation before I came to Warrington I was asked to take up this agitation. It was stated, I think, by Councillor Pea- cock, that I seek popularity. I never took it up with that idea.

Councillor W. ROBERTS: Personal spleen! Councillor DODDS : There is not a gentleman who believes I had any personal enmity. Councillor W. ROBARTS : It is all a lie! (Upper.) Councillor DODDS : I have proved it before in writ- ing and in speeches. Instead of seeking to get into this Council it is most hateful and distasteful to me and I shall rejoice when I can go through the door for the last time. (Applause.) I prefer to livemy life quietly.. Though I have been an ardent Radical I have never taken any active part in politics or pushed myself for- ward, because I disliked it. (Hear, hear.) As soon as I can,l shall get out of the popularity you say I have sought.

div.head: SOME OTHER COMPANIES.
div.p: SOME OTHER COMPANIES.

"With regard "said Mr. DODDS, "to Mackie's, Skel ton's, and Pearson and Knowles! It is the first time I knew that any member of the firm of Mackie and Co. was on the Council. With regard to Skelton's we found one or two gentlemen had shares,but I have always held that the small holder in a large company is not worth raising the question about." Councillor W. ROBERTS: Do you call Skelton's a large company? COUNCILLOR DODDS AND PEARSON AND

div.head: KNOWLES.
div.p: KNOWLES.

Councillor DODDS : We could have named many com- panies last they were so small and unimportant that we did not do so. With regard to Pearsonjand Knowles. The Mayor has £4OO in the company out of a capital of nearly a million pounds. No one would think of rais- ing such a case as this, but where a man has a large holding in a comparatively small company and is interested in an official capacity then I object. (Hear, hear.) With regard to my own case my position is absolutely moral, and if I had found it was the least bit illegal I should have resigned my seat to-night. (Applause.)
NUnCitiOr W. ROBERTS Why have you brought other secretaries in?

Councillor Door's: Because every secretary was a shareholder as well, and the directors have also been shareholders. With regard to the £140,000, I hope you will give me credit for doing what is fair. I said there had been a large amount of this trading by the Slate Campany, which I mentioned because it was the chief case. Mr. Roberts said after the Higginbottont case : "We public men are on our trial and so far as I am concerned neither I nor any member of my family will have any more profits from the trading of the Slate Company with the Corporation." Afterwards he said he should "go on," in the Parr Hall, and that is why I have mentioned his name in this matter and for no other reason whatever. I think there has been a great deal of time wasted to-night, and my experience of the Warrington Town Council is such that the sooner I can get out of it the better. I move the resolution in my name. councillor_PEmsEnToN seconded.

. Alderman BOLTON: Councillor 'Dodds has given us no reason why the Non-Traders should have two votes on the constitution of the inquiry board. One arbitra- tor is better than four other men. (Hear, hear.) If they will agree to that I think they will carry the wishes of this Council.

Councillor F. R. ROBERTS said he thought Councillor Dodds would agree that there were two things in the resolution which were absolutely impracticable. The first was that the Council had no right whatever to ad- minister the oath. Councillor Dopps : That is so. (Jnunillor F. R. ROBETS : These are technical points. There was the question of sub-contracttng-ITs-coutt had the power to inquire into that. They could not compel the Slate Company or Mr. Davenport to pro- duce their books and show what goods they had bought or sold. It was ultra Tires, and no use passing such a resolution. He suggested the adjournment of the debate for ?Jon-tight.

Alderman SUTTON supported the suggestion. Councillor DODDS: I shall not agree to the adjourn- ment of the motion. It has been before the Council for a month and I am going to challenge you to vote upon this resolution. We ask to select two members of the tribunal because we are four against :32 and we represent two-thirds of the great bulk of the better class of the people of Warrington, and that being so I shall not withdraw the resolution and I insist upon it being voted upon, Alderman BOLTON : Do you want to put impossibili- ties in the way of it being carried out? _
CouncillorSAMES EvAs said that the resolution gave them no alternative. He wanted to know something of the legal. tribunal. •

Councillor Donna: It is not a legal question. Councillor EVANS: Who is to pronounce judgment on the morality or legality of the trading of this Corporation? Councillor TrN.NroN: The Non-Traders. Councillor DODDS: Public opinion. AN ALDERMAN WHO HAS NO RIGHT TO SIT. -Councillor EVANS : Not at all. Public opinion might get heated and warped in its judgment. (Hear, hear.) If, he said, there had been no exaggeration certain members of the Council would find themselves in a. serious position. He heard of certain things which an Alderman of this Council had done, and if the allegations were true he said emphatically that that Alderman had no right to sit as an Alderman of the Borough. (Applause.) He thought also that Councillor Dodds should inform them who were the people they were going to select, and if they were in his (the speaker's) judgment, capable men' he should support the resolution. He should also liketti e ' Council to elect two men from 'outside, who were un- influenced by the question. Then there was the umpire. At the least they should have a County Court judge. I (Hear, hear.) .With regard to the non-traders generally he admitted their honesty of purpose but he disagreed with their methods. He thought, too, if he had been on the Finance Committeeat the time members of the Cor- poration were dealing illegally, ho should have said so and not waited until now.

Councillor PIERPOINT : I rise to a point of order. When the question came before the Finance Committee I calledattention to Rand resigned my membership of the Finance Committee on that ground. (Applause.) Councillor EVANS said Councillor Pierpoint probably thought he had done enough, but he should not have felt he had done enough until the question of illegality had come before the Council and tne public. In the days to come there must be a resolution submitted to the Coun- cil which should finally end all trading by members through limited companies. (Applause.) His own opinion was that if they were to be exclusive upon the question it would be much worse for the ratepayers of Warrington. That was the result of his experience. The moral aspect was one for the ratepayers to deal with and not the Council. Councillor Evans then drew atten- tion to the position Councillor Pemberton was in as ' soon as he entered the Council.

Councillor PEMBERTON: I have never voted at any committee meeting on such matters, and as I have said I am selling my shares. Councillor EVANS : lam not saying anything dero- gatory. div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. ROBERT PIERPOINT, M.P.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. ROBERT PIERPOINT, M.P.

At the Church of The Annunciation, Quebec-street, I London, W., by licence, on Wednesday ' afternoon, with non-choral service and no floral I decorations, the marriage took place of Mr. Robert Pierpoint, the Member for the Borough, son of the late Mr, Benjamin Pierpoint, of St. Austin's, Warring- ton, and Mrs. Marie Eugenie Wills, widow of Mr. John Wills, of Leeds. The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. A. Basil Wilberforce, D.D., Archdeacon of West- minster, and chaplain to the Speaker of the House of Commons, assisted by the Rev. H. Bickersteth Ottley, vicar of the Church of the Annunciation: The bride was given away by. Captain Gregory, R.N., and was attended by her friend, Mrs. Gregory, of Dundrun, near Dublin. The bridegroom was attended by Mr. Alfred , Gwyther, of London, as best man. Mrs. Wills was 1 naarri6d in a gown of pale heliotrope cloth, trimmed with lace, the sleeves being ornamented with long lace elbow cuffs, and she wore a bonnet of black lace arranged with pink roses and velvet ribbons. Among those present at the church ;were Mr. and Mrs. J. Blundell, Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Wildv, Mr. Fort une,Mrs. Arnes, Airs. Woods, Miss Edwards, Mr. C. P. Brabazon, Mrs. M'Whirter, Mts. 11. Corbett, Colonel' Brookfield, M.P., Major Rasch, M.P., Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bast., Sir Archibald Lamb, Bart. Mrs. Whalney. S. Faules, I Mr. J. Knight, Captain and Mrs., Tartley, &c. After- wards Mr. and Mrs. R. Pierpoint, left for the Continent i for a short time, and will afterwards pay a visit to Warrington. , ! The flag at the Conservative Club was displayed in ! honour of the event.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. DANIEL JONES.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. DANIEL JONES.

• Many Warrington people will deeply regret to hear of the death of Mr. Daniel Jones, which occurred at his residence, 51, Wilson Patten-street, early ‘on Saturday morning. The deceased gentleman, who was a native of Warrington, was held in high esteem by a large circle of townspeople. He was sixty nine years of age and had resided in Wilson Patten-itreet for over nine- teen years. He had been in a delicate state of health for more than twelve months, but had not been confined to the house very long. Mr. Charles White was his medical attendant. Paralysis was the cause of death. Mr Jones was twice married and leaves a widow, two sons and two daughters with whom the greatest sympathy will be felt in their bereavement. For many years the deceased gentleman was connected with the firm of Messrs. George Artingstall and Com- pany, Wildeispool-road. When 22 or 23 he became traveller for the firm and on the death of Mr Artingstall the business was left in the hands of Messrs. Warburton ' Hartley and Jones. •Mr Jones retired four or five years ago, relinquishing his position as managing director. The deceased gentleman was never a member of the Town Council, but for several years he was a poor- law guardian, and took a great interest in the work. He had been associated with the Old Men's Christmas Dinner, and Aged Women's Tea Committee for about 20 years, probably more, and at the time of his death he was one of the vice-presidents. He was many years ago one of the wardens at St. Paul's Church and at *both the morn- ing and evening services, on Sunday, the Vicar alluded to the deceased's former connection with the parish,and said he was sure the family would have the sympathy of the congregation in the sad loss they had sustained. Mr. Jones took a very deep interest in the Gymnasium. He was vice-chairman of the Building Committee and chairman of the Gymnasium Committee until five or six weeks ago, when he retired in consequence of his con- tinued ill health.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at Hill Cliff e Burial Ground on Tuesday afternoon, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton conduct- ing the service. The chief mourners were Mrs. Jones (widow), Messrs. William and A. G. Jones (sons), D. J. Dunn, Daniel Jones. William Dunn, Arthur Jones, and G. D. Dunn (grandsons), Fred Parsonage, Ben Parson- age, and J. J. Dunn (sons-in-law), and Messrs. Fred Johnson and John Jackson representing Messrs. G. Artingstall, Compajd, Limited. Amongst those present were :—Xlderman Sutton, Counz cillor James Evans, Mr. Kinsley, Mr. Hugh Ferguson, and Mr. John Hesketh, representing the Christmas Treat Committee and the Gymnasium Committee ; Mr. T. J. Ridgway, solicitor to the deceased; Dr. Bmide. medical adviser; and Messrs. D. Garnett, J. Johnson, James Hatton, and J. G. Hatton. Floral tributes were received from the following ;—Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Jones and family. Mr. and Mrs. H. Ferguson, Mr. and Mrs. Hes- keth,, themaids at the house, Mr. and Mm. J. J. Dunn and family; Lizzie, Nellie and Dan (giandchildren), Dr. and Mrs. Braide Casimir Watkins (nephew), employes of G. Artingslall and Co.,Ltd.,Mr. and Mrs. L. A. Voisey, Mrs. Lewis Voisey, Mr. J. F. and Miss Kiernan, and Alderman T. H. Sutton. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. W. C Nicholson, on behalf of Messrs. R. Garnett and Son, Sankey-street.
MR. JONES'S CONNECTION WITH THE
GYMNASIUM.

Councillor TINNION made an allusion to the death of Mr. Hanle' Jones at the tenth annual musical drill and gymnastic display held in the Gymnasium on Monday evening. He said that up to November last Mr. Jones was President of the institution, and he was a member of the first committee which was formed fourteen years ago. He had done more than any other man in thetown to further the best interests of the Gymnasium. He (Councillor Tinnion) was sure that those present would not only appreciate along with the Committee, the ser- vices Mr. Jones had rendered, but they would feel that the town had suffered a very serious loss by his death. He (the speaker) would like to convey an expression of the sympathy of that meeting to the widow and family. The audience signified their approval of this course.

At the Widnes Police Court on Monday morning, James \Tarley, 25, • Longford-street, Warrington ; Rariy MeCormiek, 13, Princess-street,Latchford ; and Robert Reed, 213, Knutsford-road, Warrington, were each fineot 2s-6d. and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly at Widnes on Saturday evening last. ,

SOUND ADVICE TO STUDENTS. Prizes Distributed at Heathside Continuation School.

Some sound advice was given to the students at St. Paul's(Heathside)Evening Continuation School on Th urs- daylast week, when the annual prize distribution took place. It is interesting to note that the school is one of the largest continuation schools for boys and Men only I in England. There was a good attendance at the prize distribution, and the students entered into the proceed- ings with enthusiasm. The Vicar (Rev. W. Bracecamp) presided, and the prizes werd distributed by Mr. J. Fulton Smith. Mr. J. H. Smethurst, Mr. H. P. Hughes, Mr. J. W. Parker (head master) and members of the teaching staff were also present. The VICAR said they were present to give prizes to those who had earned them by 'their hard work and good behaviour at the continuation school. He ,wanted them all to realize how important continuation schools , were. A greet many lads when they left school I felt that they knew everything and that they had finished their education, whereas when they left school their education was only just beginning. The instruction they received at the day school- was the ground work and when they went out into life they had to learn a I great many more things. The knowledge which they gained by attenaing evening classes would enable them I to get on in the world. Those continuation schools were, he believed, the largest men's schools in England. He did not know what the future of the schools would ) be.So far as the Education Bill was concerned they did not know where they were. He hoped that whatever , changes took place would be for the better, that the I schools would continue to grow, and that they would find young men and lads willing to come and learn. With regard to the prizes, some of them had been given by a fribnd of education, Councillor Dodds. The very ' fact that he had given the booksand encouraged so many stu&ants to attend the classes, was a proof that he was a friend of education. They were sorry that he was not present, but they could congratulate themselves upon the fact that the gentleman who was present to dis- tribute the prizes, Mr. Fulton Smith, was also interested in education, because he not only did a great deal for the schools personally, but the firm with which he was connected also did a great deal, and appreciated the work of those who attended the classes as was evidenced by the fact that they were Ailing to help the lads to come. They were pleas J. that Mr., Hughes, who represented another large, m—Messrs. I Richmond and Co.—was also present. ( atinuing the revigentleman expressed:the hopethatthr ,adents would Bake advantage of every opportunity of • ..provingtheir positions, and show themselves Worthy t. f them by carry- ing out what they learnt at their scha,ols. They were all . pleased to have a gentleman like Mr. John Parker as head of the schools. (Applause.) M. Smethurst and he (the Vicar)¼ were present t 'represent the managers and they appreciated Mr. Parker's work very much indeed, not only in connection with the day schools but also in connection with the continuation schools He believed it was owing to Mr. Parker and his noble staff of workers that the schools had gained' such efficiency. The Vicar concluded his remarks by urging the students to persevere in their work. Before distributing the prizes, Mr. J. FULTON SMITH delivered a short speech. He said it was many years since he was at a prize distribution but he had a very keen remembrance of the prize distributions in his early days. The remembrance was that he never got, a prize. (Laughter.) They were not all gifted and he was not gifted. He however, found out that if he stuck to his work that work was appreciated. He adopted as his motto "Let the work tell," and he had never regretted doing s. If the students had got that idea into their mind.thcy would never fail. He hoped they would not be dNcouraged when they found certain studies hard and difficult. He advised them to study privately as well as at the classes, because if they did not do so the classes would not seem to give them very much help. From what he had heard, Mr. Parker was one of the most efficient teachers in the town. To have an efficient teacher WAS to have one of the best foundations for making good scholars, because the teacher could communicate his own enthusiasm to the scholars. If they carried out the instruction they received and studied earnestly, the result would be satisfaction to Mr. Parker, and a reward to each of them in after life. (Applause.) Mr. FULTON SMITH theß distributed the prizes, the following being the recipients :—Winners of special prizes presented 'by Councillor J. Dodds: J. Penning- ton, G. Stokes, T. 'Hughes, J. Hilton, A. Pownall, and J. Dolphin. Winners of prizes presented by the school: J. Ashworth, A. Ashbrooke, E. Bloor, F. J. Dowling, J. Glover, W. Gibson, W. Griffiths, T. Gregory, W. Hooker, H. James, T. div.head: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
div.p: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances undertake to return the manuscripts which are not used.

div.head: "Excessive Punishment " at Runcorn.
div.p: The "Excessive Punishment " at Runcorn.

Sir,—Re the case cf "Excessive Punishment at Run- corn," an account of which qtppeared in your issue last week. I desire through the medium of your paper, to voice, whilst giving all credit to the Bench as to its desire to act justly,the extreme dissatisfaction expressed generally at the verdict, but most notably so by the i parents n the district of Trinity Schools, who most heartily j sympathise with Mr. Broadbent at this par- ticular juncture. Indeed so farhas this feeling proceeded that one poor woman, in addition to others, has proffered out of her scanty store, five shilling towards the fine and other expenses. The punishment may, or may not have been excessive, but the provocation was most undoubt- edly so. It is the opinion of many that most parents having a due regard to the boy's future, and the example he ought to have set in the pre- sent, would have added their quota of punish- ment (not necessarily corporal) to that of the teacher in order that the lesson might not fail in its effect. It argues something very far wrong somewhere, when a boy of thirteen shows such disregard of the most ele- mentary principles of decent behaviour as to dare openly, without pro vocation:to incite another boy to gross insub- ordination. Such conduct seems to point to a long series of concessions dictated rather by weakness than wisdom. It would be interesting to ask if Holy Trinity Day Schools is the only field on which such prowess in defiance and annoyance has been demonstrated. Rtmcorn parents would do well to study the story of Eli, and the i fate which betel his household, since, n the Supreme Court, causes are more severely dealt with than conse- quences.—l am, &c., A SUPPORTER OP PUBLIC DISCIPLINE. The Recent Eisteddfod.

Sir,—T don't wish to weary you or your readers with a lengthy epistle but I desire to make a few remarks in reply to Mr. Cook's last letter. He has edged out of the main question at issue, which is entirely one of principle viz., the introduction of members of other choirs assist- ing competing choirs—and llas made it appear that it is a matter of personal spleen to Mr. Berrey. I do not know Mr, Berrey personally, and I am not in the habit of harbouring spite against persons with whom I am entirely unacquainted,Ld Mr. Cook seems to imply that lain afraid of Mr. Berrey. I assure him lam not. Granted that Mr. Berrey was perfectly justified in conducting Runcorn Choir, still,considering that he had a great deal to do with promoting the Eisteddfod it was NW form for him to take any active part in the competition, and I have reason to believe that it was a mere blind to put Mr. Brown's name as conductor of the Runcorn choir,as I understood he never conducted Runcorn either at re- hearsal or public performances. In spite of Mr. Cook's denial that no St. Helen's men assisted Runcorn, I have it on good authority,that some, who are not bona-fide members did assist. Certainly. the Apollo committee ought not to have exercised any voice in arranging the different "pegs" for the choirs to "hang" on as that duty should be left to the "judge." Of course I wouldn't for one moment profess to know as much about music, Eisteddfods, brass band contests etc., as Mr. Cook, as I am only a plain "Bachelor of Music," whereasj he is the secretary of a Male Voice Choir. However, I would like him to quote any first- class band contest where one noted conductor was con- ductor of almost all the bands which competed. One noted conductor may have trained the different bands, but that is another matter entirely.—Again thanking you for inserting these few remarks, I remain, yours truly, W. H. PAYTON. 12, Froghall-lane, Warrington.

Sir,—l have read with great interest the letters of Mr. Payton and Mr.. Cook respectively in regard to the recent Eisteddfod, and it is to be regreaed that such a lamentable state of affairs exists. All unbiassed ama- teur vocalists will admire Mr. Payton for the fearless manner in which he has disclosed the fact that certain local choirs compete in Eisteddfods with other than bona-fide members, and I consider that Mr. Cook has fully proved the fact cnot intentionally) by the state- ment that Mr. Berrey is not a member of their Choir, but a paid professional vocal trainer. Now Mr. Berrey has been described in the local press as the Warrington Apollo Soloist, and has competed as such in various Eisteddfods, with success. Therefore, according to Mr. Cook the Apollo Choir are guilty of the same practice of competing with other than bona- fide members, and I do not think it sportsman like of his committee to pit a paid professional vocal trainer, who has been nursinglis voice, against the workman ama- teur, say out of a coal pit or the iron works. Now sir, I would like to advise Mr. Cook and his Committee to throw professional artistes, and all other than bona-fide members, on one side, and if their object isto win, win by merit. Then,and then only, will honour follow.

I may tell Mr. Cook from my point of view this dis- closure by Mr. Payton is not " spleen," but an honour- able objection, which all choir conductors would do well to copy, and I certainly admire Mr. Payton for being a pioneer in trying to put a stop to this bad method which certain local choirs are adopting to fill up their weak places. I would like to suggest that all choir conductors in the county should frame certain rules to be adopted by all Choirs for the better government of Eisteddfods. Thanking you in anticipation of inserting this letter in your next issue, I remain, Yours Ito., A CONSTANT READER, December 17th, 1902.

Sir,—Perhaps your correspondent, the Secretary of the recent Eisteddfod, will be kind enough to enlighten me to the real truth respecting the Mixed Voice Choir Competition, of which some very astonishing rumours are going about. A member of the Apollo Choir has informed me that the winning choir should not have been allowed to compete as it was not what it was made out to be, that on the whole it could not claim the title of a Chapel Choir, but wasa mixture of a certain Opera and prize Choir Company. If this was so,and the Committee were aware of it, and still allowed them to compete against conscientious amateur choirs, I shall begin to think that Mr Payton may possibly have some solid ground in making his com- plaint. Let the Committee try to prove otherwise. Further, I think that the most ungentlemanly and sar- castic letter which appeared in answer to his justifiable

div.head: Examiner, Friday, December 19, 1902.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, December 19, 1902.
note, does not speak well for the generosity of spirit I should have expected front a local organization of this kind.

I expect the answer to this letter will be thatit is now too late to make a complaint, but I will repeat that if the Cokumittee xvereaware that the successful choir was not what it was advertised as, they were not justified in allowing it to compete.—Yours sincerely, " DROIT."

Sir,—As one who is very much interested in the cor- respondence, re the above, which has passed through the columns of your paper, I should be very grateful if you will allow me to clear theair of a few nasty allega- tions against Mr. Payton. In the first place Mr. Payton's. charge against the Runcorn Choir was in every sense correct. Of course Mr. Cook and his committee contradict this, but I pay more attention to what members of the choir in ques- tion say. Now as lam well acquainted with many mem- bers of the Runcorn Choir I happened to make a few inquiries the week following the competition and was assured in all truthfulness r(by members) that they had the assistance of certain members of the St. Helens Choir. Since Mr. Cook's letter was published I have taken the trouble (at his suggestion) to verify this and I have also been assured that they (the Runcorn Choir) have no members from St. Helens oxitheir books. Mr. Payton is accused of want of knowledge as to the rules of carrying out these competitions. I think, judging from their explanation, they were not/so sure of the point, re the conducting of different choirs. The Runcorn Choir, according to programme, should have been under the directorship of Mr. J. Brown, who holds the post of secretary to the choir, and does not even act as deputy in the absence of their conductor, which goes to prove that theywere not sure on this point. If all was fair why didn't they bill Mr. Berrey as conductor to both St. Helens and Runcorn Choirs. I think they were afraid the rules that govern "Brass Band Contests " would not carry al-these affairs, or perhaps they had not decided under which title (St. Helens or Runcorn) they should make the attempt. But I really gave them more credit than letting out a very important fact. I think Mr Cook (or, the Com- mittee who advised him) -acted rather indiscreetly in publishing the fact that Mr. Berreywas not a member of their choir, but "their paid vocal tutor, "for un- doubtedly, then two at least, of the recent prizes they have won, were gained dishonestly. These competitions are not for professionals,but purely and simply for the education of amateurs. In fact there is published on the programmes a rule to this effect. Under these conditions I hold that they have no right to the prizes they have taken, a. 4 on these occasions Mr. Berrey, has taken very promiment parts. Therefore I fail to see inthera the sportsmanlike strAightforward- ness they boast, or the honour that has followed. I should like to deal with a few other points but I don't want to trespass further on your valuable space. T hope you will see the seriousness of the allegations published against Mr. Payton and let these few facts go to press.—Yours truly, INTERESTED.

of November Ist, 1902, where Dr. Penny's report is corn- I mented.on under the heading "The accentuation of a Tannery Nuisance by the use of yeast." "Truth" for November 13th, 1902, might also give him a little light, for the Editor deals with my matter of fact, not hysteri- cal, report to the Cheshi re County Counc Land his closing words are as follows:—" The matter is now under the I consideration of the Cheshire County Council, and it is I hoped that that body or the Local Government Board will quickly awaken the Runcorn Rural Council to a sense of their duty as Sanitary administrators." If "The Lancet," the leading medical journal of the day, and "Truth," the fearless newspaper critic, speak in such plain terms, one from a medical standpoint, and the other from that of an impartial observer, surely the conceited littleness of "Enquirer" can have little weight with those so much better acquainted with the facts of the ease for even a child could detect his bumptuous folly. He has evidently been imposed upon and the ruse he gives publicity to,is well understood, in the district of Thelwall and also who originated the same. To talk of drains or sewers caus- ing a nuisanoe, the gravity of which is attested to by so ninny poor sufferers and whose opinions were verified by Dr. Penny who heard their stories and found out the cause of their complaining,is truly making the "mole- hill" into a mountain, for nowhere in the land could be found any large sewage works which could produce a nuisance of the ammeter of the one wecomplain of and which has for so tong brought darkness, disease and probably death to a bright, happy locality. The Run- corn Rural District Council dare not read my last brief letter because they were afraid to give publicity to the fact that they have practically done nothing and ignored, ' not only their own Medical Officer's suggestions, but also the recommendations of Dr. Penny which "The, Lancet" trusts "will be speedily acted upon," Now for the last paragraph in Mr. Enquirer's curiously wrought out Epistle, asking for some in- tormation about Lymm. This shows how far a lie will travel and how long it will live* The late Dr. Fox, the 'Medical Officer, in an unguarded moment made use of an expression respecting mysely which I considered libellous. He associated my name with a block of property at Lymm which I neither owned nor had any interest in, and the result was, I demanded an explanation. After a conversation with him inwhich I explained that I did not possess norhad ever possessed any property in the Lynun Local Board area, like an henourable man which he was, he at once publicly withdrew the statement and offered me a suitable apology. I hqpe this explanation will prove consoling. to the enquiring mind of your correspondent—l bear the poor fellow no ill will nor anyone else. Just at present I feel well disposed to all men, mainly through being away from the nuisance, which was practically killing me and those belonging to me, and partly owing to the fact that I am on the winning side as regards the non- traders and this nuisance business, and as on both ques- tions we have the great mass of public opinion with us, we can afford to smile and be generous, and I beg to wish "Enquirer "and all enquiring friends a happy and joyous Christmastide. Thanking you Mr. Editor and wishing you the same, I remain, your faithful servant,
, • R. A. NAYLOR. Si. Michael's House, Egerton Gardens, London. December 26th, 1902.

div.head: Mr. K. A. Naylor and "Enquirer."
div.p: Mr. K. A. Naylor and "Enquirer."

Sir,—ln your issue of the 13th you have inserted a letter signed "Enquirer" to which the public may apply his own adjectives—"insulting, hysterical" &c., ar.c. It might have been as well if this anonymous writer had enquired a little into the subject upon which he seems to speak with such mock authority, before writing the same. There is,however,some hope for such a writer, for he is so ashamed of what he has written, as to play the wretchedly contemptible and cowardly part of con- cealing his identity by using a nom de plume, while en- deavouring to vilify and indulge in personalities. It is a reprehensible practice only employed by those de- generate Britons who do not possess even a remnant of that heroism which has made our Fatherland, great, grand and glorious. I will however deal with his letter seriatim. His gentle reminder of poetry and wood blocks, as a possible motive for my sympathy. with the non-traders is amusing in the extreme; though the connection of the two is difficult to understand. In regard to the latter I have never complained about the Warrington Corporation purchasing wood blocks from other firms for the fact is, I have no disposition to grumble as we secure the largest proportion of orders for which it is our pleasure to quote in the open market. What I have protested against is the way the purchases of the Corporation are made and public attention being called to this, has revealed &state of things, which is a perfect disgrace to anyauthority and no private concern could exist if carried on in such a manner. Take the particular case of wood blocks "Enquirer" refers to. The town required 50,000. Quotations were obtained which varied some 25 per cent. This of•course is quite natural, for the blocks might be made from scores of different brands of timber which have their own special commercial value. This order was divided between the two lowest tenderers and the Corporation had a perfect right to do this and although my firm's quotations were not the highest, still I may state that the highest prices quoted were by the largest firms who are actual manu- facturers and importers, and as the block business is usually cut very fine, the difference in price can only be accounted for in the quality. The charge I have to make against the buying department of the town is not the question of giving an order to any particular firm or firms, but the large and quite unnecessary expenditure of public money ht arranging picnic parties with the pre- sumed object of inspection, which also looks suspici- ously uncomplimentary to the respectable firms supply- ing. In this case it cost the town for this absolutely useless expedition 7i per cent, on the purchase price, whereas the customary mode—when there is any doubt as to the suitablity of the material—is to have samples forwarded and the paid officials to see that the bulk is in accordance therewith. For a deputational picnic party to take a long railway journey under such circum- stances at the public expense and to spend the town's money to the extent of £35 (which lam informed was the actual figure) would suggest that it is time to use even stronger language than what has already been uttered. One of the Councillors who enjoyed this ex- cursion publicly declared he had been on similar errands to Ireland and elsewhere to inspect stone setts. It almost seems incredible that the intelligence of Warrington should be so insulted, for surely a sample of the setts would have been quite sufficient to ascertain their quality and finish, and I therefore beg to register my protest as a ratepayer against such a system,whether it is one of the ancient customs of the Corporation or not. _ _ _

now come to the question of the Longford Depot and your correspondent rather mixes up" the ratepayers pockets" as this expression was used in special refer- ence to gas. Like Mr. Monks respecting his gas expen- diture admission "Enquirer" seems to admit that a vast amount of money has been spent in experiments, but 1 certainly do not agree with his justification of this outlay. Quite the opposite; infect lam convinced the whole thing wants inquiring into. This individual, whose identity I have a grave suspic- ion of,seemsto know more about R. A. Naylor's feelings that he does of himself, for instead of my being "thoroughly ashamed" lam very proud to have had the privilege of joining the non-traders in their denun- ciations of a glaring wrong and I now regret I have beentoo moderate in the language employed and had too much respect for the parties implicated and this exces- sive mildness I fear has been taken as a sign of weak- ness.

Now for my reference to the Borough Medical Officer of Health; a gentleman I respect for tbe same reason, and quite as much as your correspondent, and a gentle- man I never have intended to " gratuitously insult." All the mention I have made to this gentleman, whose devotion to duty during the small-pox epidemic was beyond all praise, was a very slight and passing one. The Chairmen at Parr Hall mentioned something about any return to Cuerden Hall, and my reply vkaa : "that it was impossible for me to live in my own house in con- sequence or a vile nuisance existing near." I stated " had noticed in a certain street, now known as the street of the seven smells,' a stench somewhat similar, but not so strong as the ore from which we suffered,and it would be well if the audience kept their eye on the Health Committee if there was one, and their Medical Officer for fear some of their own children might be claimed, like some of the little people I had known in our district, who had been taken away, and I wondered how long the Warrington smell would be allowed." If this is an insult to a Medical Officer, I don't knowwhat an insult means, for he is the right person to whom the public have aright to look for protection. As regards " Enquir's" remarks about my antipathy to Medical Officers, I do not possess any, for I look upon them as fellow workers in the same vineyard. Replying to his ideas about the Thelwall Nuisance he is quite at sea and evidently does not know what he is writing about. There is one thing I would like to inform the public definitely about i.e. to state if he has the Local Government Board's authority for making the statement he does. Before applying thereto I want to have his answer, and they will no doubt compel 'iron, Mr. Editor,to give "Enquirer's" real name and address so that he may be officially dealt with. The local Council he mentions, is a curiosity. I am fully dealing with it in my book on the subject, and his sneering remarks about my property being the cause of even any part of the nuisance complained of, are rather out of date for the theory has long ago been exploded at the expense of the Runcorn Rural District Council. Dr. Penny, their adviser in chief employed to set at rest all baseless assertions and to find out the exact cause of the nuisance,accomplishedlboth, and any conflicting statements then existing were settled by this eminent member of a medical profession whose detailed report and analysis proved beyond a doubt what, and who was, responsible for the nuisance. He thoroughly examined Cuerden Hall premises and my property adjoining and his opinion quite coincided with Medical Officer's I had personally employed and with that of the Inspector of the authority, and here is the result of his investigation: "The sewers and drainage system of Cuerden Hall were examined and found satisfactory." He also certified that the effluents from the Council's two sewers, with which my name has so often been unjustly associated, were satisfactory and fit to be turned into any stream. Dealing with the nuisance, there is no ambiguous lang- uage used in his report, it is as plain and as emphatic as possible. The cause is the effluvium which arises frorin a septic ferment, and he distinctly states—" The efflu- vium from such matters is unquestionably dangerous and indeed a fruitful source of much fatal disease." I hope these points are sufficiently clear to the mind of oEnquirer," and I would also refer him to "The Lancet"

div.head: LETTER WRITING.
div.p: LETTER WRITING.

, It is sometimes lamented that letter writing is a lost 'art. In these days, when one may send four ounces of I written matter to any part of the country for a penny, I letters are briefer, but infinitely more numerous, than when eightpence was charged to convey a single sheet of paper from Norfolk to London—the cost of postage marked upon letters written by the poet Cowper. Cowper died in 1800, the eve of a century prolific in changes. In the days of dear postage,when travelling was also dear and deadlyslow,middle-classpe4le were content to communicate with their distant friends three or four times a year. Huge bandies of their letters still exist, and very quaint reading they are. Generally they con- sist of minutely detailed accounts of trivial circum- stances to which nobody in the rush and scramble of modern life would give a moment's attention. "Baby has got another tooth. Mary thinks of triintning her next new bonnet with cherry-coloured ribbons: They do say as how beef is like to rise the coming winter. Smith's grey mare has turned lame."• This is a genuine extract from a letter written near Frome in 1784. Now- a-days people haven't time to write unless there is some- thing of importancetb communicate, as in the follow- ing letter from Mrs. Sarah Ann Richards, of Brynhaf, Villa, Mountain Ash, Glam, dated September 9th, 1902: I —"I feel that I must express my gratitude for the great benefit I have received from Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. About three years ago I began to suger from fits of depression and sick headaches. I lost my appetite completely; was frequently attacked by giddi- ness, followed by vomiting; could get no sleep, and became too weak to walk. My stomach was unable to retain nourishment. I , consulted one doctor after another, but they all failed in their treatment of me, and I sank further and further into a state of helplessness. But about eighteen months ago, as I was expecting and wish- ing for death to put an end to my wretched existence, a friend advised me to give Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup a trial. I felt that this wh.s like clutching at a straw to save one's,self from driowning ; but to my in- , thnse surprise and joy that medicine acted on my system ' like a charm from the very first dose, and before I had finished the second bottle my recovery was complete. I now always keep a bottle of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup by me, and whenever I feel low a dose or two suffices to restore me. I recommend the medicine when- ever I have an opportunity to do so."

div.head: DRAUGHTS.
div.p: DRAUGHTS.

WARRINGTON D. AND C. C. V. RUNCORN.—A friendly match between these clubs was played on Friday even- ing last week at the rooms of the foemer, Bibby's Restaurant, Market-street, Warrington. Th 3 visitors brought a strong team of 14 players, but Warrington was only able to muster 10, so that 3 of the Runcorn team had to play the role of spectator. This match was rather closely contested, the superiority of C. Powell and G. Rowe on the sth and Bth boards turning the scale in favour of the home team. Mr. R.
