div.head: Colborne-street Baptist Church.
div.p: Colborne-street Baptist Church.

The above church was crowded to excess on Sunday last, nany being unable to find seats and the need for increased accommodation is keenly felt. The pastor oc- cupied the pulpit and based his sermon on Mark 16, ver. 16. In the course of his remarks he said that in a pre- vious sermon they had discussed the scriptural mode of Baptism and they had seen that almost without excep- tion, the whole of Christendom were compelled to admit that Baptism by immersion was not only according to the teachings of the New Testament and the early churches but was without doubt the form of Baptism practised by Christ and the Apostles. If they consulted the standard Greek lexi- con ,of the English speaking world, they would find that it was invariably rendered, to dip, to immerse, to drown, to sink, to be over head and ears, and never in a single case was it rendered "sprinkle." Such evi- dence coming, from so impartial a source was to the mind of every honest student, indisputable and conclu- sive. Similar testimony (said the preacher) would settle for ever, questions concerning Latin or French phrases. Why not so in the case of New Testament Greek. Nay he would go even further and say that the word "Babtize "could not be otherwise expressed with- out violating all the laws of scholarship and even com- mon honesty. It was cowardice and love of tradition rather than truth that was responsible for the perversion. He would, however, remind them that the mode of Bap- tism was comparatively speaking is minor point, their distinguishing note let it never be forgotten was not immersion. They did not wish to monopolise the Bap- tistry, their great distinction was that they insisted upon placing" the inward and spiritual grace" before "the outward and visible sign." They contended that a man must be a conscious possessor of spiritual life, otherwise the acceptance of the rite was nothing more , than an empty form and a vain tradition.—At the close , the pastor baptized fourcandidates. The whole service , was marked by a feeling of solemnity—Mr. Minnie° will preach to-Morrow, and on Christmas morning is adver- tised to conduct a short service. Selections from the " Messiah "are to be rendered by the Warrington Maio Voice Choir.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football. By " Ov—alist."

Fortune has smiled again on the Warrington club, and a lucky victory at the expense a Widnes was gained on Saturday. The ohomesters had all the play but Warrington got all the' 'points after a very hard struggle. Naturally Widnes folk were sorely dis- appointed, especially as the team, has of late been do- ing well, and victory over Warrington was looked forward to. But the losers reckoned without Fish, and the team that does that,usually makes a mistake which I there is ample time and opportunity to regret I afterwards. It was Fish who won the game for War- rington and all credit to him for his brilliant effort.

Football enthusiasm in Warrington has not died away, judging by the support the team had at Widnes. Quite half the big crowd at Lowerhonse Lane came from Warrington, and they were as enthusiastic as only those who have been deprived of a pleasure for a long time can be,at the first opportunity. The nine - penny return fare caused a big rush to the railways, and the two lines delivered about five train-loads of ardent Warringtonians, while there was the usual stream of pedestrians along the canal-side. If Widnes failed to get the points they got the cash on Saturday, and a big bag of e. s d. has a wonderfully consoling effect on the officials at any rate. Prayers and ,public are not pleased to the same extent, however, merely because they don't get the money.

It was rather a nice day at mot places on Saturday, but at Widnes the conditions were not so satisfactory. True, the rain kept off, but every now and then there swept across the ground a dense cloud of vapour and fumes, which might have come from the bottomless pit during a temporary raising of the lid. Where they did come from I don't know, unless the chemical workeis of Widnes are .capable of raising a small fog, in the way the Sheffield butlers are alleged to do on days when the visiting side is batting at Bramhall-lane. Anyway the players of both teams 'on Saturday were frequently enveloped in whirling wreaths of rap* through which they were barely visible to the on- lookers. Nobody took undue advantage of the mist, howeVer, to score a surreptitious try.

Coming back to the game, it was an interesting struggle. Widnes all through had a big pull forward and they were generally hovering about in the vicinity of the Warrington line. They combined well also,and a less resolute and sound defence than Warrington's must have been broken through. But every man was in his place and being somewhat faster than the Wid- nesians they generally pulled the latter up whenever. .they got unpleasantly dangerous. Though Widnes combined well, the combination was on stereotyped lines, and a good centre-threequarter would probably have turned the scale for them. The wings got plenty of passes but they were seldom openings, though Hughes should have scored at least once.

There was no score at the interval, and it seemed anybody's game,for the Warrington men were always to lie reckoned with when near the line. : Probably a draw would have been the result had not Fish been prowling round. Widnes got possession too easily for the Warrington combination to be effective, so that Burgess did the right thing in punting across to the left-wing. Fish was bn the spot and in -the twinkling of an eye he had collared the ball and threaded his way through the home backs and scored behind the posts. It was a magnificent effort, such RS only Fish is cap- able of. Some black-hearted Widnesiim took the oppor- tunity of applying his foot to the scorer while on the ground, but he recovered and kicked the goal right enough. Five minutes later a Widnes forward foully laid Hallam out by a charge. Curtis was singled out as the offender and sent off. Widnes now, with seven forwards, pressed harder than ever and Hallam and Co., had an anxious time. They cleared, however, and before the close, Fish was right for another try when the soft turf played him false and he fell. The game finally ended in Warrington's favpur by 5 ,points to nil.

As I have already admitted, Warrington were lucky, but their defence was too good for the Widnes attack and when a chance did come their way it was taken. The team that takes chances generally wins,and Widnes have to lament a few that were not taken advantage of. The match on Saturday was productive of four points, as it counted in the South-West Lancashire Competition in addition to the League.
The South-West Lancashire League up-to-date is as follows :-- Points

The League table up to date is as follows : For Agst.

Halifax still keep at the head of affairs, and their victory over Hull was a good performance. There is nothing brilliant about the Halifax lot, but they are sound, and one secret of their success may be found,in the fact that they have established a training school for their players in the centre of the town. A spaci- ous building, which was formally used as a boiler- making establishment, has been cleared of all its fittings, laid with spent logwood, and made into a fine open hall, in which players can rnn, pass, and kick irrespective of the weather. The end walls of the building are painted to represent goal posts, so we may expect some more Wonderful goals from Little 's foot. Dressing and bath accommodation is also provided_

' Once upon,a time the Warrington men practised in the gymnasinm, and they would be none the worse for some extra training now. By the way, Diellenson,whO is such a fine kicker, ought certainly to practice the art of both dropping and placing goals. A centre who can drop a goal at a critical moment is a treasure. I have not forgotten the valuable man Cross was, in this respect, and all his skill was the result of special training and practice.

Runcorn fairly celebrated their return home on Saturday, when the Rovers were swamped by 21 points to nil. Butterworth, Price, and Walker fairly ex- celled themselves on the attack. Salford just won at Oldham, while Broughton Rangers wiped out the "gallant youths." Wigan helped themselves to two points from Brighouse Rangers, while Hunslet treated St. Helens much the same as they recently treated Warrington.

To-day Bradford are due at 'Warrington, when there is sure to he a huge crowd--granted decent weather. Warrington should win, but much depends on the for wards, whose weakness is more apparent every match- They are far too light for the work. The team will again have the assistance of Boardman and Dickenson, both of whom hai,e been badly missed, the latter especially. Bradford are not playing well just now and on Saturday were beaten at home by Huddersfield, but. this. fact is not worth much in sizing up the encounter at Warrington. I hope we shall win, if it is only for the sake of the anxious spectators who, have had such a scarcity of home matches.

div.head: WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK. A Successful Year's Work. ;
div.p: WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK. A Successful Year's Work. ;

Mr. William Long presided at the annual meeting of this bank,held at the Savings Bank, Buttermarket-street, on Tuesday morning. There were also present: The Revs. Canon Willis, John Yonge, A. S. Cameron, H. V. Pigot, and F. A. Screeton, Aldermen Sutton and Fran- comb, and Messrs. F. Monks, H. Roberts, J. A. Ransom°, J. Longland, George Thompson. John Dewhurst, T. Birchall, John Geddes, Edwin Woods, George Dakin, J. R. Young, John Harrison, JamesHepherd, C. Jackson Holmes, with Thomas Tunstall (actuary.) THE ANNUAL REPORT AND ACCOUNTS.

_ The annual report was signed by Mr William Long (chairman), and Mr. John Geddes (vice-chairman), on behalf of the 'Committee of Management. It read as follows :—`• In presenting the general statement of ac- counts of the bank for the year ended 20th November, 1902: the Committee of Management have much pleas- ure in drawing attention to the very satisfactory pro- gress of the business of the bank. 865 new and renewed accounts have been opened during the year, making the total number of depositors 13,251. 26,641 'transactions were recorded as compared with 25,228 last year; show- ing an increase of 1,413. £1,189 3s 10d has been in- vested for depositors during the year in consolidated stock, and in consequence the amount due to depositors has decreased by the sum of £332 Os. The amount now I due to depositors is £351,991 Os 3d, inaddition to which I there are investments on their behalf to the extent of , £14,434 ISs 5d in stock. The assets of the bank are £358,361 48 11d, showing a surplus of £6,3701 4s Bd, after deducting the whole amount ' due to depositors. The National Debt Corn- missionera hold on behalf of the institution a sum of £353,330 Bs. Id., which is considerably in excess of the total liabilities. The extracted list of. depositors' balances, certified by the Auditor, is placed on thecoun- I ter during the hours of business, and any depositor may satisfy himself, by its inspection, that the amount to his credit, in accordance with his pass beok, is certified to the Governmeet. The bank is open daily for the trans- : action of bru3iness, and sums as. low as one shilling are f received. Fifty pounds may be deposited in any one year until the amount to the credit of the depositor reaches £2OO. A further £2OO may also be received in any year for investment in Governmentstock. Payments not exceeding £lO are made on demand ; larger amounts are paid subj..ct to a week's notice. The continued steady increase in the number of depositors' accounts, and in the number of transactions, is a most gratifying feature of the work of the bank. The greater propor- tion of the trans ictions are of small amounts, which shows that the bank is tak.n advantage of by the class of depositors for who benefit the institution was estab- lished in the year 1818. There are 5,633 depositors, whose accounts do not exceed 21." The report of Mr. Arthur Bennett, the auditor read as follows ;—"Market Gate Chambers, Warrington, 25th November, 1902. To the truatees and managers of the Warrington Savings Bank. Deer sirs,—l have pleasure in reporting that r have completed mv audit of the books of the bank for the year ended 20th November. 1902, and hereby certify that the accompanying general statement and balance sheet are correct. I have attended the hank month by month during the year, and have checked the additions of the cash receipts and payments', proved the accuracy of the ledger postings, examined the vouchers, compared all communications from the National Debt Commissioners which affected •the accounts with the entries in the general ledger, and verified the balances in the hands of the 'treasurer. I have also frequently attended for the purpose of corn- paring depositors' pass books with the respective ledger accounts, and have tested 1,657 during the year, and found the same to agree." The CHAIM!" inquoving the ddoption of the state- ment of accormts, observed that the report NM drawn up chiefly at the instance of their admirable actuary,and gave the meeting in as short and as succinct a form as possible.the work of the bank during the past 12 months —a work that had been done in a quiet and unobtrusive way,lmt which was none the less efficient on that account (Hear, hear.) They were doing a work which in a quiet way was promoting temperance and self-respect amongst the working classes. Some little effort was being made —and he hoped it was, becoming a greater effort each year—in stemming the tide of waste and intemperance, from which Warrington was not altogether free. The work of the bank was,perhaps,best seen at a glance from the comparative statement of the business of the insti- tution for the past 22years. Although the balance due to depositors was slightly less this year, the great thing was the number of accounts opened, the number of the transactions, end the large number of small swings that came into their hands. (Hear, hear.) That was really the work of a savings bank—that people might put their money away and know that it was safe. (Ap- plause.) They could point to a large sum they had in reserve, and to the fact that they had now a Govern- ment inspection and were practically under the guarantee of the Government. Any matter the Govern- ment called attention to they were glad to carry out as opportunity presented itself.'l Mr. JOHN GEDDAI4 seconded and the motion was atTreed to.
ifiE76SMMTTTEE Or MANAGEMENT THANKED'

The Rev. Canon WMLTS moved e resolution acknow- ledging the services rendered to the institution by the Committee of Management, He agreed with the Chair- man, he said, that they had come there not to make speeches but to do business. He was sure they owed their most heartfelt thanks to the committee for their long services and congratulated them on the work which was being done at the present time by the bank. (Hear, hear.)

Mr.Jonx DEWTITTRCT,in s,,conding the proposition, observed that they all felt that the bank was doing an excellent work from year to year. It was well managed and the depositors received good interest for the money deposited. There was no fear of anything going wrong. Film the figures which had been read to them it would be seen that the bank had been even more successful this year than before, so that they might say that thrift was on the increase in Warrington. Might that con- tinue to be the case. There was great Reed for it, and he contended that it was their duty to do all they could, as employers of labour, clergy, and teachers Of both day and Sunday schools, to urge the importance of practising thrift. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then put and carried. RE-ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND _ _ _ _ VICE-CHAIRMAN. _

Mr. F. MONKS moved that Mr. William Long be re-elected chairman and Mr. John Geddes vice-chairman for the ensuing year. . Mr. J. R. YouNo,in seconding, remarked that although the importance of the introduction of new blood had been urged it was undoubtedly on the experienced veterans that the bank must rely for its real and sound support. There was no doubt that the old and experi- enced officers constituted the vertebra of that bank, therefore it would be unwise to part with such men as Messrs. Long and Geddes. ' (Hear, hear). The motion was carried. Mr. G F.DD ES briefly returned thanks for his re-election, and said he was only too pleased to do what he could for the _bank.

--The CHAIRMAN also spoke and said as longashe could hold the confidence of the trustees and managers he would be glad to accept the appointment. He had very often taken the opportunity of trying to influence his co-employers of labour to interest themselves in their workpeople. In these days of big limited companiesthe old tie of master and man had been rather broken down, but in the country, as far as he was concerned in his small way, he tiled to keep it up as long as possible. He proceeded to relate an incident in which one of his employes had taken his advice to put anyspare money in the Savings Bank, had afterwards thanked him for advising him to do so. APPOINTMENT OF TRUSTEES AND MANAGERS On the proposition of Mr. DAMN, seconded by Mr. HEPHERD, the following managers were elected to join the trustees on the Committee of Management for the ensuing year :—The Rev. R. Greenall, the Rev. John Yonge, Mr John Harrison, Mr. Thomas Whittle, Mr Thomas Birchall, Mr George Thompson, Mr. T. B. Carter, and the Rev. G. H. Carnson.

The 'ACTUARY reported that it would be necessary to appoint anew trustee in the place of Mr. Robert Davies, who died during the year, and that the following gentlemen had ceased to be managers owing to removals or deaths, namely, the Revs. A. A. Markham, T. Bishop, E. R. Tarbuck, and P. E. Powell, and Messrs John Peers, H. E. Ransome, S. Chandley, E. W. T. Richmond, and D. Jones.

_ Mr. H. ROBERTS, moved "That Mr Charles White be appointed a trustee and Messrs. E. A. Fox, C, D. Parkinson, the Rev. G. H. Carnson, Councillor J. Ci Craik, Dr. Peacocke, Mr Herbert Woods, the Rev. W Bracecamp, Mr. Percy Densham, and Mr. Stanley Carter, managers." In doing so he said there was not a man more respected or more beloved or who took a keener interest in the welfare of Warrington, than Mr. Charles White.
Mr. C. JACKSON HOLMES seconded the proposition aud it was unanimously carried. An acknowledgement of the Chairman's services con- cluded the meeting.

div.head: HUNT. An Interesting Career.
div.p: HUNT. An Interesting Career.

The news will be received with general regret of the death of Ex-Chief Constable. Hunt who passed peacefully away at his residence, 18, Salisbury-street, shortly before noon yesterday. The deceased, gentle- man- who had reached the advanced age of seventy- four, had been in failing health for some time and a week ago bronchitis set in. He was attended by Dr. Langdale, but despite every attention, gradually sank and died at the time stated. His wife predeceased him in July, and he severely felt the blow. The late Mr. Samuel Hialt had a long and interesting connection with the Warrington Borough Police Force. On the 22nd of August, 1895, he submitted his resigna- tion to the Watch Committee, and at a meeting of that committee held on the same day, the following resolu- tion was passed, which in itself is a handsome tribute to his worth : That in accepting with regret the resignation of Mr. Hunt, the committee desire to place on re- cord their high appreciation of the efficient and satisfactory manner in which he has during a period of 29 years discharged the duties of the very im- portant office of Chief Constable of the Borough; that a testimonial to the value of £5O be presented to Mr. Hunt on his retirement from the office of Chief Constable; and that for the purposes of the Police Acts, 1839 to 1893, the services of Mr. Hunt in the force be certified to be approved service." • The following details of Mr. Hunt's long connectioni with the police force.of the town will be read with interest. Mr. Hunt joined the Warrington police force on December 21st, 1863, as superintendent, having left the Derby borough force for that purpose. In Derby he had given a service of 13 years and 8 months, and brought with hint to Warrington first-class testimonials as to character and ability for the whole of that time - In Warrington he served nearly 32 years, so that his continuous service in the two police forces amounted irr all to a little over 45 years. When Mr. Hunt joined the - Warrington Police Force, Mr. Mac Michael was-Chief Constable. This gentleman was appointed to the office in December, 1852, and resigned in July, 1866, and On August 9th following Mr. Hunt was ap- • pointed to the position at a salary of £145 per annum. The salary was advanced at various times till 1888 when it reached £3OO per annum. The strength of the police force when he joined was 16 and the population about 26,000. At the time of his retirement seven years ago the force was 54 all told and the population 57,000. Mr. Hunt had many exciting experiences in Warrington. During the year 1866, a gang of burglars was captured and the proceeds of no fewer than 18 burglaries by them. from Warrington and other places in Lancashire and Cheshire were recovered and restored to the owners, the thieves being sent for trial and convicted. About the same time a Fenian scare took place, and it entailed a vast amount of anxiety and labour on the part of the police by night and day. A great number of special constables were placed upon duty, along with the regular policemen for the safety of public buildings and the public generally. In the following year a ter- rible railway collision at Walton Arches on the London and North-Western Railway occurred, whereby a gieat number of persons were killed and injured. Inquests on the dead lasted for weeks, and nursing and care of the injured for months. During Mr. Hunt's lengthenedser- vice there were seven Parliamentary elections in War- rington, and the disturbances which occurred at some of these caused the police to have lively times, but no serious damage to property or injury to the person resulted. The difficulties under which Mr. Hunt laboured may be judged from a letter contributed to the "Examiner" by the late Mr. George Powlson, formerly editor of the "Warrington Advertiser." "When Mr. Hunt came at the close of 1863," wrote Mr. Powlson, "the popula- tion was only about 26,000 and the police force 16, and its members were on such easy terms with the publicans of the town that many of them could go in at one door and out at another of most of these houses, levy toll on the passage, and see nothing but what was strictly cor- rect or required reporting while on the journey. Mr. Hunt came as superintendent of the police force, to revolutionise the natural product of this state of things. And what with only a partially con- verted Watch Committee, with a somnolent magis- tracy, an obstructive chief constable, a recalcitrant body of officials, and a formidable and ill-regulated criminal element among the population, he found no bed of roses ro receive him; and he had to fight his way into the respect, if not into the affections of his varied antagonists. And the marvel was that the bad- gered supenntendent did not throw up his appointment, and leave his enemies masters of the field. But there were law-loving men in the town who encouraged him to persevere ; and they had good materials to work on, and most satisfactory have been the results ! Wheh Mr. Hunt NVIIS presented with a cheque for RS& by the Corporation on his retirement in 1895, he spoke at great length, contrasting the town as it was when he first came to it with what it was at that time. In his opinion it was on the whole, one of the "best-conducted and law abiding towns" in the country. The present Chief Constable (Mr. Luke Talbot) succeeded Mr. Hunt, • and although seven years have elapsed since he com- menced his duties here, he is sometimig 411 spoken of as the "new chief constable." In Mr. Tawet, the town has got a worthy successor of, Mr. Hunt and one whd- sots up to its hest traditions.

BITING A Doo's TAIL.—FINE INFLICTED. George Welsby, of Croft, appeared at the Warrington County* Petty Sessions on Wednesday in answer to a summons charging him with ill-treating a dog on November 29th.—James Lodge, landlord of the General Elliot Hotel, Croft, stated that at 9,30 p.m. on the date in question defendant came into the house. Witness was keeping a beagle puppy belonging to Mr. Wood, of Newton, anddefendant picked theanimal up and fondled it. Witness had occasion to leave the room but on hear- ing the dog howling returned. On examining the animal he saw that a portion of its tail had been taken off.— Aaron Marsh stated that he saw the defendant bite the end of the dog's tail off.—Evidence was given by P.C. Callaghan and Inspector Print and the severed portion of the tail was produced in court.—Defendant made hia 46th appearance, but the Bench decided to treat him elniently and imposed a fine of 5s and costs.

The other day a football was put to a singular, not to say severe, test in a town not a thousand miles from Burslem. MUNICIPAL TRADING.--Continued from Page G. tary of an honourable company trading with the Cor- poration. Was it fair to the Corporation and the colliery proprietors that the prices of tenders should come before him? A QUESTION OF FACT BETWEEN COUNCILLORS TINNION AND PEMBERTON. Councillor TINNION said Councillor Dodds had given them no reason why they should have an inquiry on his lines. Councillor DODDS : Public opinion. Councillor TDINION : I wits returned by the elector- ate just the same as you. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) Ile would strengthen the resolution by not only having the inquiry for the period mentioned, but up to the pre- sent, the 31st December. There were some people just as guilty as others who had recently come into the Coun- cil (Hear, hear). The non-traders had said they could do without an inquiry. The other evening he hada long conversation with Councillor Pemberton, and asked him what he would say if the tribunal brought in a verdict of "Not Guilty." Coulicillor Pemberton said: " I should not believe it. Ithas been done so cleverly that we could not find it out. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON: That is not true! . Councillor TnvroN (turning to Councillor Pember- ton): You said it to me on Monday week last in the committee room after the meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee when I spent two hours with you. lam surprised to hear you deny it. Continuing, Coun- cillor Tinnion asked if it was possible that a man like Councillor Pemberton should be one of the five to adjudicate. He would agree to nothing that would give '• Councillor Pemberton a standing of that kind. (Hear, hear.) He would not vote for the resolution unless he knew who the men were. They should not be judge, ' jury, and accusers as well. (Applause). Alluding to the oath, he said the officials and servants of the Corpora- tion were the only people who could be put upon oath, and he would not agree to such an indignity being put I on them. Councillor Tinnion finally, appealed for a committee to determine the character of the inquiry. 1 Councillor PEMBERTON: I solemnly deny ever using 1 the words imputed by Councillor Tinnion. It will be a 1 warning to me never again to have any private conver- sations with Councillor Tinnion. The DEpirry-IVIAYoR : At every Council and Com- mittee meeting youhave either been called a liar, or you have called somebody else a liar. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON : I am in a terrible minority, but I did not think a man would say what ia not true as the result of a private conversation. Councillor TINNION : It was not a private conversa- tion. I asked him point blank. Councillor TugsfoN then repeated his assertion Circumstantially. Councillor PEMBERTON : I never went back on any- thing I said in my life. Councillor F. R. ROBERTS: Mr. Pemberton has already been convicted of slandering me. . ALDERMAN SUTTON'S RED HERRING. Councillor PIERPOINT: These personalities are not to the credit of the Council of Warrington. They had had a series of whitewashing speeches. He was one of 36 members who had been charged by the non-traders with certain incriminating circumstances and he did not fear any inquiry that could be made. He wanted no whitewashing speeches on his behalf. They were prisoners at the bar of public opinion in Warrington' and he did not think the prisoner as a rule was allowed to select his own judge or form of trial. Alderman Sutton tried as well as he could to draw a red herring across the trail, but he was not so clever as he thought, and it made him (Councillor Pierpoint) wonder whether he had not some purpose in constantly drawing the red. herring across the path. He was going to vote for Councillor Dodds' resolution because he was sick and tired of the agitation. They (the Council) were a dis- credited body-- Councillor F. R. ROBERTS: Question? Councillor PIERPOINT: Question! That is another red herring. (Laughter.) He thought tbe question was settled at the meetings in Parr Hall and on the Ist of November. (Applause). He was ready to vote for and come before any tribunal. (Cries of "So am I.") MORE COUNSEL'S OPINION. Councillor DODDS replied to Councillor James Evans' i.• speech, with regard to his own position. The business his firm did with the Corporation was done from an agency office in Liverpool and in the 25 years he had been secretary he had never seen a single tender to the Gas Committee, and the contracts had never come before bun except when sealed by the Company He was not a member of the CtftB Committee and he would leave the Finance Committie if necessary. (Applause.) He had taken Counsel's opinion twice and he knew he was right ' legally and morally. His remuneration did not depend : in any way uponthe business done with the Corporation., Councillor W. ROBERTS: When did you sell your shares? Councillor Dorms: About 15 months ago. If Coun- cillor Roberts thought he had the slightest idea of com- ing into the Council he 'could assure him he was wrong. He wanted to get out, and he would do if he had the slightest doubt of his position. Councillor JAMES EVANS said if the question was left an open one they were where they were. Tf *t was • made exclusive the whole moral question must ~• con- sidered. He wanted it to be exclusive and not a qustion of percentage or how much trading. He moved the 1 adjournment of the meeting. 1 ' Alderman SUTTON: It was moved an hour ago. Councillor DODDS: I shall not raise the question again. Alderman SUTTON: We are not going to be dictated to. The amendment for an adjournment was then voted upon and lost by 15 votes to 12. RESOLUTION CARRIED. The DEPLYTV-MAYOR then put Councillor Dodds' re- solution, and the voting was as follows:— For Coun. Dodds' motion. Against. Councillor Bennett, Alderman Sutton, . 9 f Hulse, If SmetL Davies, ,i. , Hutchinson) i ff ft PP ft Barton, Bolton, NI J. Roberts, Councillor F. R. Roberts. • JP Dodds, ' „ Peacock, „ Lipson, ~ W. Roberts, „ Brophy, „ Duncan, , „ (Intik, . ~ Ellison, Pemberton Sampson, e I ft a Wilkinson, • ~John Evans, Ift Rogers, „ and the I Pt Pierpomt, „ Chairman. 1 13 12 The motion was therefore carried. CONFIRMED BY THE COUNCIL. Alderman SUTTON: Th4s ,will have to be confirmedat the next monthly meeting of the Council. The TOWN CLERK: We can go back to Council now if weWish. Alderman SUTTON and several other members were already leaving the chamber when Councillor PIERPOINT rose, and proposed that the meeting resolve itself into an ordinary meeting of the Council. Councillor TESNION seconded and it was carried. Councillor DODDS then moved his resolution again and i'-• Councillor PEMBERTON seconded. . The DEPUTY-MA YOR put the motion and it was carried by such an overwhelming majority of the members left, Ant there was no apposition. This terminated the business and the, members dis- persed.

SERIOUS FIRE AT RUNCORN. £3,000 Damages. An alarming lire was discovered shortly after nine o'clocck on Friday evening, to have broken out in the printing works of Messrs. R. Moore and Co., High-st' , by a girl named Katie Mullard. The fire brigade under Superintended Wright, was quickly on the scene and aided by a good supply of water, soon began to combat the flames. Llnlucki ly the fire had gained a good hold before the brigade arrived,and for sometime their efforts had to be directed to prevent the flames from spreading. As it was midnight had arrived before the fire had been mas- tered, and not until some £3,000 of damage had been done—fortunately covered by insurance. The fire is supposed to have been caused throug:h a spark from a lighted stove. During the fire Superintendent Wright sustained rather a severe injury fo his hand. Theplace is completely wrecked, and it is extremely lucky that in spite of the high wind, the fire did not travel into the adjoining houses and shops.
